use_notes: Belavadös DOCX and ZIP files supply world lore, race families, creator-god doctrine, daily-life tone, and time conversion data.
Uploaded spell JSON and grimoire ZIP supply spell names, classes, casting fields, level tags, and school tags.
Uploaded D&D PDFs are used only for generalized play, adventure, encounter, monster-reference, and errata structure patterns; their named NPCs and locations are not imported.
The uploaded reference image is treated as a visual attachment with no additional rules text needed for these JSON outputs.

named_content_policy.rule: D&D book content is generalized only; named NPCs and named locations from uploaded D&D books are intentionally omitted.
applies_to: spell display names/descriptions when names contain setting-person eponyms
named_content_policy.does_not_remove: Belavadös setting terms, Belavadös deity names, ancestry names, system-neutral race/class terms, or player-facing rules terminology.

expansion_source_inventory.rule_policy: Uploaded D&D books are generalized only; named NPCs and named locations from D&D book sources are not imported. Belavadös-original names, deities, factions, races, constellations, and settlements may be retained as setting canon.

world_overview.setting_frame: A dark steampunk fantasy world shaped by industrial expansion, ancient horror, political infrastructure, and fragile systems trying to hold civilization together.
world_overview.tone: Dangerous but not hopeless. Horror, bureaucracy, industrial decay, discovery, humor, resilience, and human-scale kindness all coexist.
world_overview.living_world_principle: The world continues through regions, factions, discoveries, conflicts, and player decisions instead of a single fixed storyline.

morning: Check Earth-first time for work, transit, market openings, school, court, temple, or crew schedules.
Check Belavadös companion date for festivals, legal records, sky omens, religious observance, and local paperwork.
Prepare tools, spell components, travel papers, work badges, fare tokens, oxygen or pressure gear where needed, and emergency coin.
daytime: Most people work around infrastructure: rail yards, docks, skyship towers, record offices, food markets, schools, clinics, repair shops, foundries, farms, guild halls, and arcane maintenance crews.
A quiet life still touches danger through inspections, taxes, rationing, delayed shipments, power failures, divine-prison rumors, missing ledgers, and local faction pressure.
Adventurers spend the same hours following leads, preparing routes, interviewing witnesses, guarding cargo, crawling ruins, or taking jobs too unstable for ordinary agencies.
evening: Families and crews return by rail, ferry, walking route, animal cart, skyship shuttle, or local service line.
Taverns, shrines, station halls, guild rooms, common kitchens, and boarding houses become rumor exchanges.
Night travel is possible but more expensive, more heavily policed, and more exposed to weather, undead irregularities, predators, and bureaucratic mistakes.

daily_effects: Schedules matter because work, courts, medical appointments, spell services, freight, and adventuring deadlines depend on them.
Infrastructure is both mundane and arcane; a transit delay can be a mechanical failure, a weather problem, a labor dispute, a magical surge, or a sign of something worse.
Tickets, permits, cargo ledgers, death records, and identity papers are part of daily survival, not background decoration.
adventure_hooks: A shipment arrives with the wrong legal identity attached.
A quiet station records a passenger who never boarded.
A skyship crew refuses to land after seeing something below.
A rural line keeps running exactly on time after its staff disappear.

ichor_in_daily_life.definition: Ichor is the harvested divine substance that powers medicine, alchemy, necromancy, industry, ritual work, poisons, curses, political influence, and elite economies.
public_face: Clinics may use refined treatments that citizens depend on but distrust.
Factories, laboratories, and noble institutions treat ichor access as power.
Ordinary people may never see raw ichor, yet still live under systems funded or stabilized by it.
social_consequences: Dependency creates corruption because institutions benefit from keeping imprisoned gods useful rather than ending the system.
Black markets grow around exposure, feeding rights, refined powder, miracles, and false cures.
Class divides sharpen between people protected by licensed ichor systems and people harmed by extraction, experimentation, debt, or unsafe work.
ichor_in_daily_life.safety_guidance_for_table: Use ichor as infrastructure, temptation, medicine, weapon, evidence, and moral pressure. It should create choices, not force one correct answer.

divine_prisons_and_religion.daily_presence: The imprisoned gods are not distant myths; their prisons, cults, harvest economies, temple records, and political bargains shape daily life.
divine_prisons_and_religion.public_story: Authorities frame the prisons as protection for civilization.
divine_prisons_and_religion.uncomfortable_truth: Civilization also turned divine predation into an industry that many institutions rely upon.
ordinary_believers: Some pray out of fear, habit, family tradition, gratitude, coercion, or practical need.
Some reject worship but still use calendars, oaths, medicine, records, and social systems built around the gods.
Some families carry blessings, marks, curses, obligations, or inherited proximity to divine systems.

law_records_and_death.ledger_of_death: Death is recorded with supernatural precision. When records fail, reality and society both destabilize.
daily_effects: Inheritance, burial, identity, marriage, taxes, debt, and legal standing depend on records staying accurate.
Clerks, priests, doctors, undertakers, guards, and family witnesses become essential civic roles.
A small paperwork error can become horror when the dead, missing, or wrongly recorded return to the story.
law_records_and_death.adventure_or_quiet_life_use: A quiet clerk, grieving family, or exhausted station registrar can matter as much as a battlefield hero.

classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.barbarian: Seen as survivalists, shock troops, storm-workers, bodyguards, labor champions, or people whose rage is cultural, spiritual, trauma-born, or elemental rather than simple anger.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.bard: Messengers, performers, negotiators, propagandists, historians, spirit-speakers, morale workers, and dangerous keepers of memory.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.cleric: Temple workers, field medics, record keepers, exorcists, community anchors, or divine-system specialists who may serve faith, institution, or necessity.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.druid: Ecological repair workers, rural protectors, plague watchers, weather readers, rot-cycle tenders, and critics of industrial overreach.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.fighter: Soldiers, guards, duelists, escorts, strikebreakers, union defenders, militia leaders, and practical survivors.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.monk: Disciplined adepts, infiltrators, temple-trained specialists, couriers, body-mind healers, or shadow workers depending on tradition.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.paladin: Oath-bound enforcers, reformers, protectors, zealots, rescuers, or state-sanctioned champions whose oath may clash with law.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.ranger: Scouts, route wardens, monster trackers, rural guides, border workers, transit pathfinders, and settlement protectors.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.rogue: Investigators, spies, burglars, survival criminals, locksmiths, smugglers, auditors, assassins, or people who understand systems from beneath them.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.sorcerer: Innate magic carriers whose bodies or bloodlines make them valuable, feared, recruited, licensed, or exploited.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.warlock: Pact-bearers whose bargains can be personal, political, ancestral, desperate, institutional, or hidden.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.wizard: Scholars, engineers, necromancers, auditors of reality, ritualists, professors, infrastructure mages, and dangerous specialists.
classes_and_multiclasses_in_society.multiclass_life: Multiclass characters are often people whose life crossed institutions: a medic who learned battlefield magic, a scholar drafted into temple service, a guard trained by monks, or a laborer whose pact solved an impossible debt.

factions_and_class_pressure.factions_as_daily_systems: Factions are not only quest-givers. They are employers, unions, temples, ministries, black markets, research circles, noble blocs, neighborhood networks, transport authorities, and secret societies.
class_divides: The wealthy buy privacy, treatment, transport priority, legal insulation, and safer magic.
Workers face unsafe industry, delayed pay, surveillance, rationing, exposure, and forced compromises.
Rural and isolated communities often rely on neighbors, practical skills, barter, and dangerous local bargains more than central authority.
Adventurers can move between classes but are rarely free of debt, reputation, permits, sponsors, or consequences.

adventuring: Adventuring is irregular work that may include investigation, escort, ruin delving, monster response, sabotage, rescue, diplomacy, courier duty, and disaster recovery.
Adventurers are useful because they can cross social boundaries and take risks institutions cannot publicly admit.
Their choices can change trade, law, faction influence, public trust, and the safety of ordinary people.
quiet_living: A quiet life is possible and meaningful: farming, repair, teaching, clerical work, healing, cooking, childcare, fishing, ferry work, smithing, music, scholarship, or tending the dead.
Quiet characters still have agency through relationships, testimony, expertise, shelter, rumor, labor action, ritual help, and refusal.
Belavadös treats ordinary logistics as story: food arriving late, an inheritance form missing, a train canceled, or a clinic denied supplies can begin an adventure.

ancestry_and_biome_life.race_file_connection: The race JSON supplies creator families, likely biomes, unlikely visitor biomes, alignment tendencies, and table abilities.
biome_effects: Ocean, plains, mountain, forest, and hybrid environments shape accents, jobs, clothing, food, hazards, architecture, transport, and prejudice.
Unlikely biomes do not forbid a character; they mark visitor status, migration, pressure-sealed housing, diplomatic travel, special gear, or unusual life history.
Creator-god doctrine affects social records and temple interpretation, but player choice can always move beyond inherited expectations.

player_onboarding.new_players: No system mastery is expected. Start with what the character wants, what they fear losing, who they protect, and what kind of trouble they are willing to enter.
player_onboarding.experienced_players: Expect layered politics, consequences, infrastructure, custom races, long-term continuity, and moral pressure without requiring encyclopedic setting knowledge.
player_onboarding.table_culture: Collaborative, patient, communicative, and welcoming. Boundaries, comfort, accessibility, and shared storytelling matter more than perfect performance.

ordinary_problem_table: A legal record contradicts lived reality.

paragraphs: Life In The World Of Belavadös
The Hungry Gods Await
A living atlas of weather, gods, peoples, ichor, transit, work, death, monsters, festivals, and ordinary survival beneath two moons
The painted face of Belavadös: drowned shelves, reef-bright coasts, green continents, island chains, and high storm mountains.

This guide is written for anyone arriving in Belavadös with a need to understand the place before it misunderstands them. It treats the world as a living society: roads obey rain, ports obey moon-pull, class identity carries public reputation, monsters reshape markets before they threaten bodies, and ordinary people survive by reading sky, rot, transit, and law together.
Contents
1. Entering the Living World
2. Sky, Time, Moons, and the Star-River
3. The Imprisoned Gods and the Pantheon
4. Peoples, Bloodlines, Alignment, and Social Reading
5. Disciplines, Multiclass Lives, Adventuring, and Quiet Work
6. Ichor, Thundercoil Craft, and Divine Industry
7. Transit, Public Infrastructure, and Travel Law
8. Geography, Water, Weather, and Vertical Law
9. Biomes, Food, Homes, Childhood, and Daily Life
10. Death, Resurrection, and the Ledger
11. Creatures, Ruins, and Monster Signs
12. Factions, Law, Economy, and Quiet Living
13. Festivals, Constellations, and Seasonal Rhythm
14. Journey Cues, Hazard Clocks, and Ordinary Days
15. References and Sources
1. Entering the Living World

Belavadös is warm, wet, crowded, divine, rotten, engineered, and hungry. It has no white polar crowns; the far ends of the world are living coast, dark water, wet cliff, fog reef, rain-polished stone, and long forest. Ice exists where sun and ordinary weather cannot command it: in abyssal ice-crowns, pressure shelves, cold brine vaults, mountain remnants, brief harbor skim, and wandering omenbergs that frighten ships far from any cold horizon.

The world is not passive scenery. Weather has memory. Roads obey rain. Ports obey moon-pull. Factions obey transit. Class identity is a job, a social reputation, and a survival method. Monsters are not only combats; they are map terms, warning stories, food-chain pressure, disease vectors, divine traces, and reasons why settlement borders bend.

Every settlement lives by at least three clocks: the sun-year, the silver moon, and the copper moonlet. In industrial regions, a fourth clock joins them: the ichor inspection ledger. A person living in Belavadös learns to ask not only whether a road is open, but which moon is pulling, whether the skyship has cooled, whether the bridge fungus has been scraped, whether the temple bells have rung, and whether the nearest prison-god has been fed recently enough to remain weak.

The phrase most strangers learn first is not a blessing. It is a warning: The Hungry Gods Await. It means the divine powers of the world are real, imprisoned, exploited, and still starving. It means civilization survived the Gods by turning them into infrastructure. It means the greatest achievements of the age are also the greatest evidence of its moral failure.
Living Rules Every Traveller Learns

A person who thrives here does not ask whether the world is dangerous. They ask which danger is ordinary, which danger is seasonal, and which danger is a sign that a god, faction, beast, engine, or tide has begun moving beneath the surface.
2. Sky, Time, Moons, and the Star-River

Belavadös orbits within a relatively flat shared plane called the Celestial Road. Its year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days. Civil calendars keep eleven named months of thirty dates, while skykeepers, tide-priests, navigators, and observatory clerks track the small drift with temple clocks and harbor ledgers. Traveller-facing schedules may keep ordinary travel dates, but in-world record keepers translate them into Belavadös dates, moon phases, tide warnings, and sky omens.
Eleven Civil Months and Their Sky-Record Themes

The bright band crossing the night sky is the Star-River of Belavadös. In a world without modern skyglow, it is not a faint haze but a major geography of darkness, silver, dust, and rivering light. Farmers use it to time planting songs. Sailors use it as a sky-road. Funeral registrars use it as proof that the dead still pass beneath witnesses. Children learn that a promise made under a named constellation is never private.

Chandratecu-Seleneš is the great silver-white moon, broad enough to dominate public calendars and tide stairs. Mictlindra-Nannara is the smaller copper-gray moonlet that remains near the silver moon and races through a quicker cycle. Together they create layered tides: the large moon makes the public rhythm, while the copper moonlet adds fast pulses that can turn ordinary water into a sudden law of survival.
The Two Moons
Named Tide States

The constellations are the old sky-names used before the Gods were imprisoned and before industrial ichor taught cities to trust engines more than stars. They retain fixed positions and are used for sky maps, temple records, route watches, oath ledgers, birth signs, trial nights, and festival timing. Each constellation carries a practical calendar use as well as a mythic one.
Constellations and Their Festival Uses

Constellation holidays are not isolated feasts. They are civic instruments. Bastveig's Tidehook closes reef gates for pilgrim tides. Ishtanora's Hearthdrum opens village storehouses and harvest kitchens. Enkirael's Warfire legalizes certain contests of arms while making unsanctioned duels easier to prosecute. Nephthysra's Mirror turns reconciliation into public art, while Freyseth's Mask blesses disguises, confessions, and threshold bargains. Nefarokir's month is feared because funeral ledgers, death debts, and resurrection petitions are audited together.

The most dangerous coastal days are not simply storm days. Danger rises when wind, pressure, rain, and moon-pull stack together. A modest storm can flood a harbor on a Copper-Silver King Tide; a powerful storm can spare a road on a Hushed Neap.
3. The Imprisoned Gods and the Pantheon

The Gods of Belavadös are ancient creators, predators, patrons, and prisoners. They shaped mortal peoples from design, hunger, curiosity, beauty, war, utility, and dominion. Their open reign ended only a few generations ago. The prisons that hold them are not merciful tombs; they are feeding engines, suppression systems, and extraction chambers built by rulers who chose control over liberation.

Ichor made the decision corrupt. Divine blood could heal disease, strengthen magic, extend life, fuel engines, empower curses, alter minds, preserve food, ignite industry, mutate bodies, and enrich elites. Destroying the Gods would have freed the world from divine predation, but it would also have collapsed the economies and miracles that depended on them. The ruling powers chose to keep the Gods alive, hungry, weakened, and harvestable.

This is why faith in Belavadös is complicated. A shrine may protect a village, a temple hospital may save a child, a god-mark may explain ancestry, and an ichor-fed train may bring medicine through a flood. None of that makes the Gods benevolent. The world lives in the aftermath of a victory that immediately became an industry.
Creator Gods, Peoples, and Dominions
Prison-era religion
Temples are often public service centers: they record deaths, teach letters, heal wounds, certify oaths, regulate festivals, and interpret moon-tide calendars.
Prison cults divide into loyalists, reformers, abolitionists, harvest-right advocates, anti-ichor radicals, and court-aligned extraction houses.
Noble houses may display old divine blessings while privately funding stronger prison locks.
Common people may pray to a god they hate because the harvest, fever, tide, or birth still falls under that god's old pattern.
Clerics are not automatically trusted; many are evaluated by which prison, faction, or service ledger they serve.
Divine House Rites and Social Functions
4. Peoples, Bloodlines, Alignment, and Social Reading

Every people in Belavadös carries a creator-god tradition. That inheritance is not destiny, but it matters. It shapes myths, prejudice, ritual custom, common occupations, marriage law, adoption law, military expectation, divine backlash, and the way strangers read a face at a border office. Mixed heritage is common enough to have legal frameworks, but rare combinations still attract temple attention, faction recruitment, and street superstition.
Four-axis alignment

Belavadös does not compress morality into a single label. It uses four independent axes from 0 to 3000, with 1500 as the true neutral center and normal movement in 250-point steps. A person can be lawful but exploitative, cooperative but pragmatic, honorable while rejecting authority, or generous while chaotic.
Four Alignment Axes

The phase bands matter in play: 0-999 is extreme negative, 1000-1499 is skewed negative, 1500 is true neutral, 1501-1999 is skewed positive, and 2000-3000 is extreme positive. Alignment records in Belavadös are used by courts, temples, guilds, faction recruiters, and some magical ledgers, but they are descriptive rather than absolute. A person can change through acts, pressure, corruption, grief, divine exposure, and chosen community.
Bloodline families as social worlds

Humans and mixed-heritage peoples are treated as bridge cultures, valuable in diplomacy and suspicious when courts demand purity. Elven peoples carry moonlit, forest, wilderness, and hunter associations. Dwarven and gnomish kin are bound to craft, invention, stone law, and underground halls. Smallfolk cultures often control hearth trade, grain roads, inn law, and humble but crucial rural diplomacy. Orcs, goblinoids, giantkin, and draconic peoples are too often flattened into stereotypes by frightened cities; in Belavadös they possess their own law, poetry, engineering, food culture, kinship, and moral arguments.

Planar, undead, fey, elemental, psionic, construct, avian, beastfolk, aquatic, aberrant, plant, shadow, experimental, primal, and rare peoples are all part of everyday civilization. A rail station may include a warforged signal officer, a merfolk tide advocate, a goblin cook, a triton customs inspector, a tabaxi courier, a mycelian physician, a changeling actor, a dragonborn magistrate, and a dhampir death registrar without requiring the scene to become exotic. The world is strange; its bureaucracy is stranger.
Mixed heritage and cultural inheritance

Mixed heritage is handled through parentage, cultural upbringing, and creator-god resonance. Not every mixed person expresses every physical trait. Some inherit a visible body mark, some inherit social standing, some inherit resistance or vulnerability, and some inherit only the burden of being read incorrectly by everyone else. The most respected communities keep mixed-heritage registrars who understand adoption, chosen family, donor lineage, divine ancestry, and magical transition.
5. Disciplines, Multiclass Lives, Adventuring, and Quiet Work

Disciplines in Belavadös are not merely practical roles. They are professions, reputations, guild categories, temple expectations, school traditions, and public risks. A wizard may be a professor or a battlefield accountant. A rogue may be a criminal, a lock inspector, a salvage diver, or a perfectly licensed legal specialist. A barbarian may be a ritual warrior whose rage is a sacred weather-state rather than a lack of discipline.
Public Disciplines and Social Roles
Multi-discipline training as a life path

Multiclassing is common among mature adventurers because Belavadös demands hybrid competence. A storm cleric who learned wizardry can read weather as math and prayer. A rogue with ranger training can move through legal paperwork and marshland with equal ease. A fighter who becomes an artificer may understand both battlefield cost and machine maintenance. A druid-paladin may defend a river with law, oath, and root systems together.

Quiet life still contains class identity. A retired fighter runs bridge drills for children. A bard keeps market contracts audible and memorable. A monk teaches breath exercises to pressure divers. A warlock runs a threshold shop where no bargain is spoken without witnesses. Adventuring is not the only destiny of power; it is the loudest one.
Adventuring economy

Adventurers are tolerated because they go where institutions cannot act quickly. They cross closed tide roads, negotiate with monster-sign communities, recover records from drowned halls, escort ichor inspectors through angry towns, enter ruins before official survey teams, and take blame when a court wants plausible deniability. In return they receive money, favors, relic shares, transit priority, healing vouchers, faction attention, and enemies with excellent memories.
6. Ichor, Thundercoil Craft, and Divine Industry

Ichor is divine bioelectrochemical fluid: living residue, electrolyte, sacred contaminant, fuel, medicine, narcotic, mutagen, battery, and political leverage. The safest systems separate, dilute, bond, cool, ground, measure, and meter it. The most dangerous disasters occur when opposing fractions touch directly, membranes tear, catalysts overheat, prayer resonance overloads, or the living divine residue begins behaving as if it wants something.
Ichor States, Uses, and Dangers

The engineering sentence every apprentice learns is: Ichor is not lightning in a bottle; it is divine hunger forced into an electrochemical bookkeeping system. That sentence is painted above workshops because it warns against both superstition and arrogance.
Thundercoil craft

Thundercoil devices translate charged ichor into controlled cyan arcs, contact discharge, pressure bursts, and overload effects. They appear as hand weapons, bows, rifles, shotguns, grenades, coil arrays, axes, hammers, swords, daggers, and ship-scale systems. Their cultural role is larger than combat: they are symbols of industrial modernity, class fear, worker danger, military escalation, and the public argument over whether divine suffering should power ordinary tools.
Handheld Thundercoils are regulated by charge capacity, maintenance seals, permit class, and visible cyan readiness glow.
Quiet coil-bows and scouting weapons are favored by rangers, skyship lookouts, and covert marsh patrols.
Coil arrays are area-denial platforms, training rigs, ship defenses, and desperate last-line machines.
Every overload has a social aftermath: witnesses, repair ledgers, injury claims, faction questions, and temple arguments.
Illicit Thundercoil parts often contain impure ichor, false saintglass, stolen prison residue, or forged inspection marks.
7. Transit, Public Infrastructure, and Travel Law

Belavadös is not a world where travel is a blank line between scenes. Travel is public law, weather calculation, class contact, faction leverage, and divine technology. Passenger times are settlement-local. Each 15 degrees of longitude equals one public hour from Belavadös Meridian Time, and portal travel still produces local clock jumps even when the crossing itself is quick.

All public routes depend on inspection culture. Faster transit is never free. Ichor multiplies power density and shortens routes, but it adds cooling time, legal handling, membrane checks, grounding plates, prayers no engineer admits are necessary, and the risk that a delay becomes a faction opportunity.
Public Transit Modes
A day on public transit

A commuter in Belavadös checks the sky before the timetable. They leave home beneath a roof still wet from night condensation, pass a fungus-scraper clearing a bridge post, and read the station board for weather holds, tide delays, ichor inspections, and local-time conversions. The train bell may say the route is open, but the ferry gate may close at Copper-Silver King Tide, the skyship may need an extra grounding cycle, and a portal hall may suspend crossings if the destination lock hears an omen bell.

Transit creates social mixing. A monk shares a pressure lift with reef merchants. A warforged conductor argues with a human fare clerk about sleep rights. A triton passenger carries water in a legal bladder. A rogue legalist buys a licensed violence bond in the same building where a cleric stamps flood relief forms. The station is not scenery; it is the modern face of the world.
Terminals as civic organs

Stations, harbors, docks, locks, skyports, submarine halls, and portal chambers are where government becomes physical. They contain customs desks, prayer alcoves, cooling yards, public clocks, food stalls, warning boards, guild offices, faction watchers, medical benches, lost-child posts, corpse registrars, and rumor markets. A transit map is a political map disguised as convenience.
Settlement Design and Travel Law
Transit Hazard Clock
8. Geography, Water, Weather, and Vertical Law

Belavadös is a wet, broken, living map: broad green continents cut by inland seas, drowned shelves, reef lace, island chains, high storm mountains, trench roads, and forested coasts. Every blue expanse is road, food source, divine depth, weather engine, monster habitat, and legal border.
Great Regions at a Glance
Cartographer’s Paint Key
Painted Map Biome Families
Complete Named Water Layer

The names below are the atlas layer used by pilots, tide-priests, fishers, farmers, caravan masters, and mapmakers. Local villages may keep smaller names for ponds and footbridges, but these are the world-facing waters used in law, trade, warnings, and stories.
Major Oceans and World-Shaping Seas
Water Words Used by Belavadös Cartographers
Province Water Names
Abyssal Ice-Crowns, Deeps, and Omenbergs

The deep cold of Belavadös is not a white lid over the world. It is a hidden under-architecture. The abyss holds blue-black ice-crowns, hydrate stone, cold brine lakes, mineral chimneys, sleeping eggs, pressure-slow microbes, and god-sealed vaults.

When trench walls crack or deep currents lift fragments, an omenberg can appear far from any place that feels cold enough to make ice. Such bergs can carry freshwater, poison, old bones, living spores, alchemical salts, or the sound of the pressure shelf that birthed them.
Abyssal Places
Omenberg Kinds
Complete Named Landform Layer

The visible land of Belavadös is a chain of green masses, coastal shelves, mountain needles, wet forest, marsh, and volcanic ribs. Each province keeps its own named highlands and living landmarks, but the names below are the broad atlas layer used across borders.
Province Mountains, Volcanoes, Forests, and Landmarks
Island Chains and Monster-Marked Landmarks
Named Weather Formations
Weather in Belavadös has names because weather has memory. A storm that returns every season becomes a road tax, a festival, a warning bell, a monster story, and eventually a legal doctrine.
Weather Names and Meanings
Province Governance and Transit Identity
Province Atlas
Province Climate Atlas
Each province is a weather country. The map’s painted colors, province borders, settlement biomes, water edges, and vertical records all shape its local life.
Province Climate Atlas, Part One
Province Climate Atlas, Part Two
Province-by-Province Field Notes
Each province below is given as a traveller might remember it: by water, terrain, weather, vertical reach, and the kind of daily difficulty that shapes local manners.
Aelvanyr

Aelvanyr belongs to the sunbelt reef-wet belt. Its named water is Rootglass River and Mythraelyn Delta, and its broad sea or bay is Wildbloom Sound. The terrain leans toward Partial forest, Farming, Deep forest. Travellers watch for Root-rain Lanterns. The highest recorded settled weather band reaches 4600 m and the deepest recorded route reaches 180 m. Expect canopy thunder, fungus bloom, dripping calm.
Aelwynora

Aelwynora belongs to the sunbelt reef-wet belt. Its named water is Seleneš Glasswater Sea, and its broad sea or bay is Elarithen Pearl Bay. The terrain leans toward Beach and grass with water, Partial forest, Ocean Surface floating settlement. Travellers watch for Silver-Salt Fog. The highest recorded settled weather band reaches 1200 m and the deepest recorded route reaches 6200 m. Expect salt haze, floating docks, moon-tide fog.
Astraevos

Astraevos belongs to the sunbelt reef-wet belt. Its named water is Vaelunthir Mirror Gulf, and its broad sea or bay is Astraevos Reefcourt. The terrain leans toward Beach and grass with water, Beach and reefs with water, Partial forest. Travellers watch for Mirror-Squall Line. The highest recorded settled weather band reaches 220 m and the deepest recorded route reaches 4800 m. Expect mixed coast and inland weather.
Bravelyn

Bravelyn belongs to the sunbelt reef-wet belt. Its named water is Loxvire Emberwash, and its broad sea or bay is Qasvire Southreach. The terrain leans toward Beach and grass with water, Beach and reefs with water, Partial forest. Travellers watch for Ember-Heat Dryline. The highest recorded settled weather band reaches 1200 m and the deepest recorded route reaches 4800 m. Expect mixed coast and inland weather.
Ceulrithan

Vertical Weather: Heights and Depths

Belavadös weather is vertical. A city may have a salt harbor, cliff farms, skyship ledges, cave roads, and submarine locks under the same name. The tallest settled weather bands reach 5,200 m, while the deepest recorded routes descend to 8,200 m. One province can have ridge lightning, reef fog, and abyssal cold in a single trade cycle.

9. Biomes, Food, Homes, Childhood, and Daily Life

Life in Belavadös is abundant, but abundance is not comfort. Warmth speeds roots, rot, insects, fever, harvest, mold, and hunger. Communities survive because they work with the weather rather than against it. The best buildings drain, breathe, shade, flex, lift, close, reopen, and accept that repair is not failure but civic rhythm.
Biome Settlement Life and Infrastructure
Biome Weather and Settlement Response
Food, clothing, and housing

Food culture is preservation culture. Salt fish, smoked roots, fermented grain, pickled reef vegetables, fungal breads, pressure-dried kelp, hard travel cheese, spice-sealed stews, and temple-stamped emergency cakes are common. The wealthy eat fresh fruit year-round because they can buy cooling charms and sealed transit; the poor eat what survives humidity.

Clothing is layered for wet heat, sudden storm, mud, insect pressure, and transit safety. Reef settlements favor quick-drying wraps and shell clasps. Caverns favor treated wool, leather, brass fasteners, and lamp-reflective trim. Cities mix formal silhouettes with practical ventilation. Travelers carry spare socks, waxed bags, salt packets, fever charms, and a written local-time conversion if they expect to cross longitude bands.

Housing is elevated, ventilated, limewashed, drained, and repairable. Roofs are steep where rain hits hard, flat only where they are inspected often. Marsh homes stand on raised walks. Reef homes use waterlocks. Cavern homes use condensation gutters. Treetop homes flex in wind. Rich houses may hide divine wards in beautiful plaster, but even poor homes keep a dry shelf for documents.
Education and childhood

Children learn sky, tide, rot, and route safety as basic literacy. A child may learn the four alignment axes before formal grammar because courts, temples, and guilds use them. They learn which monster names are literal and which are warnings. They learn that the big moon is not alone, that bridges need scraping, that a pretty cyan leak is not a toy, and that a god can be both imprisoned and dangerous.
10. Death, Resurrection, and the Ledger

Death in Belavadös is active. The death god maintains a design, a sequence, and a ledger for every living creature. Every soul has an appointed moment written into reality. Whenever someone escapes that fate through luck, magic, prophecy, intervention, or coincidence, the design fractures. The god of death responds not as a passive judge but as a force that hunts correction.

Unconsciousness is not merely blood loss. Reaching the edge of death means the ledger has noticed the soul personally. Candles gutter, clocks stutter, rain may begin, mirrors may crack, animals may panic, and nearby witnesses may hear distant funeral bells. A failed death save is death tightening its grasp; a success is not triumph but theft.
Resurrection as cosmic debt

Resurrection magic exists, but it is not a clean reset. It may save a beloved life while moving pressure elsewhere. It may attract ledger-auditors, corpse rumors, omen animals, dream summons, or divine correction. Temples record resurrections as public spiritual events because an escaped death can change more than one person's fate.
A natural recovery can still leave a soul marked by cold memories, grave dreams, or a new fear of mirrors.
A resurrection may require witnesses, debt payment, a vow, a journey, a returned name, or a bargain with a hostile ledger.
Undead are not all the same: some are curses, some are debts, some are grief, some are legal mistakes, and some are deliberate resistance.
Necromancy is judged by context: funeral preservation, battlefield abuse, ancestral consultation, corpse labor, and resurrection theft are not treated equally.
Death festivals are part mourning, part audit, part appeasement, and part defiance.
Funeral culture

Funerals vary by biome. Reef funerals may release weighted lanterns into tide roads. Cavern funerals carve names into condensation stone. Farming villages bake memory bread and distribute it before rot can claim the grain. Treetop families hang bells where the wind can speak. Cities file death certificates with temple, court, and transit office because an unresolved death can close roads, inheritances, and magical permissions.
11. Creatures, Ruins, and Monster Signs

Belavadös treats monsters as ecological and social facts. A monster may be a citizen, a plague, a holy sign, a market hazard, a faction asset, a weather metaphor, a food-chain pressure, a criminal partner, a legal category, or a reason a road was never built straight. outside-rule creature material is used as a bestiary language, but each creature is translated into Belavadös weather, gods, transit, death, and ichor logic.
Creature Families and Belavadös Integration
Monster Words Used as Ecology, Weather, and Map Terms
Ruins, undercities, and buried works

Deep ruins in Belavadös are not empty mazes waiting for heroes. They are failed infrastructure, buried temples, prison-adjacent service tunnels, drowned archives, collapsed rail works, fungal cities, abandoned noble laboratories, old monster lairs, refuge networks, and places where weather can no longer leave. A good ruin has supply logic, waste routes, air, water, silence, old maps, new occupants, and at least one faction that wants the truth delayed.

Undercities matter because warm wet worlds build downward as often as upward. Mountain provinces carry deep cavern settlement networks. Coastal cities hide old flood levels beneath new markets. Dead stations become smuggler roads. Tombs become fungus farms. Dwarves, drow, tieflings, shadow peoples, miners, pressure engineers, and all those who prefer stone to sky make underlayers into real neighborhoods rather than background darkness.
Wilderness travel

Wilderness travel uses free movement, negotiation, ruin crawls, guerrilla routes, survival pressure, political encounter, and monster ecology. A lost-world island may preserve older beasts. A canyon may use rope and pulley law. A rainforest ruin may be more alive than abandoned. A reef may be an open-air ruin that floods twice a day. Every path should ask: who maintains it, what season breaks it, what creature reads it better than people do, and which faction profits if travelers vanish?

12. Factions, Law, Economy, and Quiet Living

Factions are living Belavadös powers: offices, cults, orders, syndicates, institutes, courts, machine-priesthoods, and public-service bodies. They attach themselves to routes, permits, settlement danger, province government, resident peoples, and access to ichor. A job becomes public when transit, rumor, paperwork, and witness culture make secrecy too expensive.
Factions as Public Pressure
Settlement Scale and Everyday Population Feel
Legal crime and public violence

Some provinces recognize forms of registered violence, salvage rights, prize shares, cleanup bonds, target classes, collateral declarations, and witness fees. This does not make crime safe; it makes it bureaucratic. A rogue may need better paperwork than a paladin. A killing may be illegal in one district, taxable in another, and spiritually catastrophic in both.
Economy of daily work

Belavadös economies are based on food preservation, route maintenance, ichor licensing, repair labor, weather prediction, transit access, monster-response contracts, temple services, document drying, salvage law, and faction patronage. The most important workers are often not glamorous: bridge scrapers, roof menders, tide clerks, apothecaries, condenser cleaners, route translators, corpse registrars, signal operators, waterlock attendants, and public cooks.
Quiet living

Not everyone is an adventurer. Most lives are made of water collection, roof repair, family meals, transport fares, gossip, worship, work shifts, market bargaining, seasonal dread, and small pleasures. Quiet people know which fungus is edible, which clerk is kind, which road floods, which station clock lies, which faction recruiter smiles too much, and which constellation makes their grandmother whisper. The chronicle world feels large when ordinary people have reasons to live that are not simply waiting for heroes.
13. Festivals, Constellations, and Seasonal Rhythm

Belavadös festivals follow the overlap of month theme, constellation witness, tide state, agricultural need, faction interest, and local disaster memory. A holiday is never only decorative. It opens markets, closes roads, suspends debts, permits masks, launches pilgrimages, changes patrol levels, alters transport loads, and tells ordinary people what danger society has agreed to notice.
Festival Types and Civic Effects
Seasonal Calendar of Belavadös

Constellation holidays are civic instruments. Bastveig's Tidehook closes reef gates for pilgrim tides. Ishtanora's Hearthdrum opens village storehouses and harvest kitchens. Enkirael's Warfire legalizes certain contests of arms while making unsanctioned duels easier to prosecute. Nephthysra's Mirror turns reconciliation into public art, while Freyseth's Mask blesses disguises, confessions, and threshold bargains. Nefarokir's month is feared because funeral ledgers, death debts, and resurrection petitions are audited together.
14. Journey Cues, Hazard Clocks, and Ordinary Days

Journeys in Belavadös are shaped by weather signs, local law, transit delays, monster movement, public mood, and the quiet labor of people who keep roofs, ferries, bridges, lamps, ledgers, and bodies working.

rows: Beholders, mind flayers, neogi, cranium rats, intellect parasites, alien oozes
Signs of psychic weather, ancient mistakes, and thought-hunger. Their lairs bend maps, memory, sleep, and authority.
Hill, stone, frost, fire, cloud, and storm giants plus giant-kin
Not merely big people: they are vertical climate events. Their migrations alter pasture law, road tolls, and mountain weather.
Goblins, hobgoblins, bugbears, orcs, gnolls, war bands
Used as cultures with logistics, songs, cooks, veterans, messengers, and treaties. Raids are political weather, not random noise.
Green hags, sea hags, night hags, covens, curse brokers
Live where desire and desperation become law. A hag market can offer medicine, revenge, love, or ruin at the same stall.
Kobolds, lizardfolk, yuan-ti, dragonborn neighbors, dinosaurs
Reptilian life is tied to heat, lineage, memory, tunnel craft, and old draconic claims. It appears in swamps, reefs, deserts, ruins, and court law.
Ghosts, wights, revenants, vampires, ghouls, skeletons, death-touched folk
Undeath is a legal and spiritual breach. It may be tragedy, curse, debt collection, divine oversight, or deliberate resistance.
Fairies, changelings, satyrs, redcaps, quicklings, dream-touched wanderers
Fey are not cute distractions. They are contracts, moods, roads, names, masks, and stolen time given bodies.
Dinosaurs, giant insects, cave fishers, gricks, cockatrices, rothe, aurochs
Large beasts shape farming and route law. Cockatrices turn entire valleys cautious; dinosaurs make some islands feel like older worlds.
Kraken-priests, sea spawn, sahuagin, merfolk, tritons, reef predators, leviathans
The ocean is a nation of pressure, hunger, and gates. Some sea monsters are citizens; others are weather with teeth.
Warforged, relicborn, animated armor, clockwork guardians, living transit systems
Constructs are people, tools, evidence, and crimes depending on who built them and whether the soul inside consented.
Mycelian minds, mandrakes, wood woads, vegepygmies, awakened roots
Rot is infrastructure. Fungus networks remember foot traffic, dead gods, spilled ichor, and old bargains.
Aasimar, tieflings, devils, demons, curses, emissaries
Planar bloodlines are not outside the world; they are the world admitting a border has been crossed.

sections.heading: Life In The World Of Belavadös
The Hungry Gods Await
content: A living atlas of weather, gods, peoples, ichor, transit, work, death, monsters, festivals, and ordinary survival beneath two moons
The painted face of Belavadös: drowned shelves, reef-bright coasts, green continents, island chains, and high storm mountains.

This guide is written for anyone arriving in Belavadös with a need to understand the place before it misunderstands them. It treats the world as a living society: roads obey rain, ports obey moon-pull, class identity carries public reputation, monsters reshape markets before they threaten bodies, and ordinary people survive by reading sky, rot, transit, and law together.

9. Biomes, Food, Homes, Childhood, and Daily Life
12. Factions, Law, Economy, and Quiet Living
14. Journey Cues, Hazard Clocks, and Ordinary Days
1. Entering the Living World
content: Belavadös is warm, wet, crowded, divine, rotten, engineered, and hungry. It has no white polar crowns; the far ends of the world are living coast, dark water, wet cliff, fog reef, rain-polished stone, and long forest. Ice exists where sun and ordinary weather cannot command it: in abyssal ice-crowns, pressure shelves, cold brine vaults, mountain remnants, brief harbor skim, and wandering omenbergs that frighten ships far from any cold horizon.

The world is not passive scenery. Weather has memory. Roads obey rain. Ports obey moon-pull. Factions obey transit. Class identity is a job, a social reputation, and a survival method. Monsters are not only combats; they are map terms, warning stories, food-chain pressure, disease vectors, divine traces, and reasons why settlement borders bend.

Every settlement lives by at least three clocks: the sun-year, the silver moon, and the copper moonlet. In industrial regions, a fourth clock joins them: the ichor inspection ledger. A person living in Belavadös learns to ask not only whether a road is open, but which moon is pulling, whether the skyship has cooled, whether the bridge fungus has been scraped, whether the temple bells have rung, and whether the nearest prison-god has been fed recently enough to remain weak.

The phrase most strangers learn first is not a blessing. It is a warning: The Hungry Gods Await. It means the divine powers of the world are real, imprisoned, exploited, and still starving. It means civilization survived the Gods by turning them into infrastructure. It means the greatest achievements of the age are also the greatest evidence of its moral failure.

sections.heading: Living Rules Every Traveller Learns
content: A person who thrives here does not ask whether the world is dangerous. They ask which danger is ordinary, which danger is seasonal, and which danger is a sign that a god, faction, beast, engine, or tide has begun moving beneath the surface.

sections.heading: 2. Sky, Time, Moons, and the Star-River
content: Belavadös orbits within a relatively flat shared plane called the Celestial Road. Its year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days. Civil calendars keep eleven named months of thirty dates, while skykeepers, tide-priests, navigators, and observatory clerks track the small drift with temple clocks and harbor ledgers. Traveller-facing schedules may keep ordinary travel dates, but in-world record keepers translate them into Belavadös dates, moon phases, tide warnings, and sky omens.

sections.heading: Eleven Civil Months and Their Sky-Record Themes
content: The bright band crossing the night sky is the Star-River of Belavadös. In a world without modern skyglow, it is not a faint haze but a major geography of darkness, silver, dust, and rivering light. Farmers use it to time planting songs. Sailors use it as a sky-road. Funeral registrars use it as proof that the dead still pass beneath witnesses. Children learn that a promise made under a named constellation is never private.

Chandratecu-Seleneš is the great silver-white moon, broad enough to dominate public calendars and tide stairs. Mictlindra-Nannara is the smaller copper-gray moonlet that remains near the silver moon and races through a quicker cycle. Together they create layered tides: the large moon makes the public rhythm, while the copper moonlet adds fast pulses that can turn ordinary water into a sudden law of survival.

sections.heading: Named Tide States
content: The constellations are the old sky-names used before the Gods were imprisoned and before industrial ichor taught cities to trust engines more than stars. They retain fixed positions and are used for sky maps, temple records, route watches, oath ledgers, birth signs, trial nights, and festival timing. Each constellation carries a practical calendar use as well as a mythic one.

sections.heading: Constellations and Their Festival Uses
content: Constellation holidays are not isolated feasts. They are civic instruments. Bastveig's Tidehook closes reef gates for pilgrim tides. Ishtanora's Hearthdrum opens village storehouses and harvest kitchens. Enkirael's Warfire legalizes certain contests of arms while making unsanctioned duels easier to prosecute. Nephthysra's Mirror turns reconciliation into public art, while Freyseth's Mask blesses disguises, confessions, and threshold bargains. Nefarokir's month is feared because funeral ledgers, death debts, and resurrection petitions are audited together.

The most dangerous coastal days are not simply storm days. Danger rises when wind, pressure, rain, and moon-pull stack together. A modest storm can flood a harbor on a Copper-Silver King Tide; a powerful storm can spare a road on a Hushed Neap.

sections.heading: 3. The Imprisoned Gods and the Pantheon
content: The Gods of Belavadös are ancient creators, predators, patrons, and prisoners. They shaped mortal peoples from design, hunger, curiosity, beauty, war, utility, and dominion. Their open reign ended only a few generations ago. The prisons that hold them are not merciful tombs; they are feeding engines, suppression systems, and extraction chambers built by rulers who chose control over liberation.

Ichor made the decision corrupt. Divine blood could heal disease, strengthen magic, extend life, fuel engines, empower curses, alter minds, preserve food, ignite industry, mutate bodies, and enrich elites. Destroying the Gods would have freed the world from divine predation, but it would also have collapsed the economies and miracles that depended on them. The ruling powers chose to keep the Gods alive, hungry, weakened, and harvestable.

This is why faith in Belavadös is complicated. A shrine may protect a village, a temple hospital may save a child, a god-mark may explain ancestry, and an ichor-fed train may bring medicine through a flood. None of that makes the Gods benevolent. The world lives in the aftermath of a victory that immediately became an industry.

sections.heading: Prison-era religion
content: Temples are often public service centers: they record deaths, teach letters, heal wounds, certify oaths, regulate festivals, and interpret moon-tide calendars.
Prison cults divide into loyalists, reformers, abolitionists, harvest-right advocates, anti-ichor radicals, and court-aligned extraction houses.
Noble houses may display old divine blessings while privately funding stronger prison locks.
Common people may pray to a god they hate because the harvest, fever, tide, or birth still falls under that god's old pattern.
Clerics are not automatically trusted; many are evaluated by which prison, faction, or service ledger they serve.

sections.heading: Divine House Rites and Social Functions
4. Peoples, Bloodlines, Alignment, and Social Reading
content: Every people in Belavadös carries a creator-god tradition. That inheritance is not destiny, but it matters. It shapes myths, prejudice, ritual custom, common occupations, marriage law, adoption law, military expectation, divine backlash, and the way strangers read a face at a border office. Mixed heritage is common enough to have legal frameworks, but rare combinations still attract temple attention, faction recruitment, and street superstition.

sections.heading: Four-axis alignment
content: Belavadös does not compress morality into a single label. It uses four independent axes from 0 to 3000, with 1500 as the true neutral center and normal movement in 250-point steps. A person can be lawful but exploitative, cooperative but pragmatic, honorable while rejecting authority, or generous while chaotic.

sections.heading: Four Alignment Axes
content: The phase bands matter in play: 0-999 is extreme negative, 1000-1499 is skewed negative, 1500 is true neutral, 1501-1999 is skewed positive, and 2000-3000 is extreme positive. Alignment records in Belavadös are used by courts, temples, guilds, faction recruiters, and some magical ledgers, but they are descriptive rather than absolute. A person can change through acts, pressure, corruption, grief, divine exposure, and chosen community.

sections.heading: Bloodline families as social worlds
content: Humans and mixed-heritage peoples are treated as bridge cultures, valuable in diplomacy and suspicious when courts demand purity. Elven peoples carry moonlit, forest, wilderness, and hunter associations. Dwarven and gnomish kin are bound to craft, invention, stone law, and underground halls. Smallfolk cultures often control hearth trade, grain roads, inn law, and humble but crucial rural diplomacy. Orcs, goblinoids, giantkin, and draconic peoples are too often flattened into stereotypes by frightened cities; in Belavadös they possess their own law, poetry, engineering, food culture, kinship, and moral arguments.

Planar, undead, fey, elemental, psionic, construct, avian, beastfolk, aquatic, aberrant, plant, shadow, experimental, primal, and rare peoples are all part of everyday civilization. A rail station may include a warforged signal officer, a merfolk tide advocate, a goblin cook, a triton customs inspector, a tabaxi courier, a mycelian physician, a changeling actor, a dragonborn magistrate, and a dhampir death registrar without requiring the scene to become exotic. The world is strange; its bureaucracy is stranger.

sections.heading: Mixed heritage and cultural inheritance
content: Mixed heritage is handled through parentage, cultural upbringing, and creator-god resonance. Not every mixed person expresses every physical trait. Some inherit a visible body mark, some inherit social standing, some inherit resistance or vulnerability, and some inherit only the burden of being read incorrectly by everyone else. The most respected communities keep mixed-heritage registrars who understand adoption, chosen family, donor lineage, divine ancestry, and magical transition.

sections.heading: 5. Disciplines, Multiclass Lives, Adventuring, and Quiet Work
content: Disciplines in Belavadös are not merely practical roles. They are professions, reputations, guild categories, temple expectations, school traditions, and public risks. A wizard may be a professor or a battlefield accountant. A rogue may be a criminal, a lock inspector, a salvage diver, or a perfectly licensed legal specialist. A barbarian may be a ritual warrior whose rage is a sacred weather-state rather than a lack of discipline.

sections.heading: Multi-discipline training as a life path
content: Multiclassing is common among mature adventurers because Belavadös demands hybrid competence. A storm cleric who learned wizardry can read weather as math and prayer. A rogue with ranger training can move through legal paperwork and marshland with equal ease. A fighter who becomes an artificer may understand both battlefield cost and machine maintenance. A druid-paladin may defend a river with law, oath, and root systems together.

Quiet life still contains class identity. A retired fighter runs bridge drills for children. A bard keeps market contracts audible and memorable. A monk teaches breath exercises to pressure divers. A warlock runs a threshold shop where no bargain is spoken without witnesses. Adventuring is not the only destiny of power; it is the loudest one.

sections.heading: Adventuring economy
content: Adventurers are tolerated because they go where institutions cannot act quickly. They cross closed tide roads, negotiate with monster-sign communities, recover records from drowned halls, escort ichor inspectors through angry towns, enter ruins before official survey teams, and take blame when a court wants plausible deniability. In return they receive money, favors, relic shares, transit priority, healing vouchers, faction attention, and enemies with excellent memories.

sections.heading: 6. Ichor, Thundercoil Craft, and Divine Industry
content: Ichor is divine bioelectrochemical fluid: living residue, electrolyte, sacred contaminant, fuel, medicine, narcotic, mutagen, battery, and political leverage. The safest systems separate, dilute, bond, cool, ground, measure, and meter it. The most dangerous disasters occur when opposing fractions touch directly, membranes tear, catalysts overheat, prayer resonance overloads, or the living divine residue begins behaving as if it wants something.

sections.heading: Ichor States, Uses, and Dangers
content: The engineering sentence every apprentice learns is: Ichor is not lightning in a bottle; it is divine hunger forced into an electrochemical bookkeeping system. That sentence is painted above workshops because it warns against both superstition and arrogance.

sections.heading: Thundercoil craft
content: Thundercoil devices translate charged ichor into controlled cyan arcs, contact discharge, pressure bursts, and overload effects. They appear as hand weapons, bows, rifles, shotguns, grenades, coil arrays, axes, hammers, swords, daggers, and ship-scale systems. Their cultural role is larger than combat: they are symbols of industrial modernity, class fear, worker danger, military escalation, and the public argument over whether divine suffering should power ordinary tools.
Handheld Thundercoils are regulated by charge capacity, maintenance seals, permit class, and visible cyan readiness glow.
Quiet coil-bows and scouting weapons are favored by rangers, skyship lookouts, and covert marsh patrols.
Coil arrays are area-denial platforms, training rigs, ship defenses, and desperate last-line machines.
Every overload has a social aftermath: witnesses, repair ledgers, injury claims, faction questions, and temple arguments.
Illicit Thundercoil parts often contain impure ichor, false saintglass, stolen prison residue, or forged inspection marks.

sections.heading: 7. Transit, Public Infrastructure, and Travel Law
content: Belavadös is not a world where travel is a blank line between scenes. Travel is public law, weather calculation, class contact, faction leverage, and divine technology. Passenger times are settlement-local. Each 15 degrees of longitude equals one public hour from Belavadös Meridian Time, and portal travel still produces local clock jumps even when the crossing itself is quick.

All public routes depend on inspection culture. Faster transit is never free. Ichor multiplies power density and shortens routes, but it adds cooling time, legal handling, membrane checks, grounding plates, prayers no engineer admits are necessary, and the risk that a delay becomes a faction opportunity.

sections.heading: A day on public transit
content: A commuter in Belavadös checks the sky before the timetable. They leave home beneath a roof still wet from night condensation, pass a fungus-scraper clearing a bridge post, and read the station board for weather holds, tide delays, ichor inspections, and local-time conversions. The train bell may say the route is open, but the ferry gate may close at Copper-Silver King Tide, the skyship may need an extra grounding cycle, and a portal hall may suspend crossings if the destination lock hears an omen bell.

Transit creates social mixing. A monk shares a pressure lift with reef merchants. A warforged conductor argues with a human fare clerk about sleep rights. A triton passenger carries water in a legal bladder. A rogue legalist buys a licensed violence bond in the same building where a cleric stamps flood relief forms. The station is not scenery; it is the modern face of the world.

sections.heading: Terminals as civic organs
content: Stations, harbors, docks, locks, skyports, submarine halls, and portal chambers are where government becomes physical. They contain customs desks, prayer alcoves, cooling yards, public clocks, food stalls, warning boards, guild offices, faction watchers, medical benches, lost-child posts, corpse registrars, and rumor markets. A transit map is a political map disguised as convenience.

sections.heading: 8. Geography, Water, Weather, and Vertical Law
content: Belavadös is a wet, broken, living map: broad green continents cut by inland seas, drowned shelves, reef lace, island chains, high storm mountains, trench roads, and forested coasts. Every blue expanse is road, food source, divine depth, weather engine, monster habitat, and legal border.

sections.heading: Complete Named Water Layer
content: The names below are the atlas layer used by pilots, tide-priests, fishers, farmers, caravan masters, and mapmakers. Local villages may keep smaller names for ponds and footbridges, but these are the world-facing waters used in law, trade, warnings, and stories.

sections.heading: Water Words Used by Belavadös Cartographers
Abyssal Ice-Crowns, Deeps, and Omenbergs
content: The deep cold of Belavadös is not a white lid over the world. It is a hidden under-architecture. The abyss holds blue-black ice-crowns, hydrate stone, cold brine lakes, mineral chimneys, sleeping eggs, pressure-slow microbes, and god-sealed vaults.

When trench walls crack or deep currents lift fragments, an omenberg can appear far from any place that feels cold enough to make ice. Such bergs can carry freshwater, poison, old bones, living spores, alchemical salts, or the sound of the pressure shelf that birthed them.

sections.heading: Complete Named Landform Layer
content: The visible land of Belavadös is a chain of green masses, coastal shelves, mountain needles, wet forest, marsh, and volcanic ribs. Each province keeps its own named highlands and living landmarks, but the names below are the broad atlas layer used across borders.

sections.heading: Province Mountains, Volcanoes, Forests, and Landmarks
Named Weather Formations
content: Weather in Belavadös has names because weather has memory. A storm that returns every season becomes a road tax, a festival, a warning bell, a monster story, and eventually a legal doctrine.

sections.heading: Province Climate Atlas
content: Each province is a weather country. The map’s painted colors, province borders, settlement biomes, water edges, and vertical records all shape its local life.

sections.heading: Province-by-Province Field Notes

Vertical Weather: Heights and Depths

Belavadös weather is vertical. A city may have a salt harbor, cliff farms, skyship ledges, cave roads, and submarine locks under the same name. The tallest settled weather bands reach 5,200 m, while the deepest recorded routes descend to 8,200 m. One province can have ridge lightning, reef fog, and abyssal cold in a single trade cycle.

sections.heading: Extreme Settlement Bands Above the Sea
Extreme Settlement Bands Below the Sea
9. Biomes, Food, Homes, Childhood, and Daily Life
content: Life in Belavadös is abundant, but abundance is not comfort. Warmth speeds roots, rot, insects, fever, harvest, mold, and hunger. Communities survive because they work with the weather rather than against it. The best buildings drain, breathe, shade, flex, lift, close, reopen, and accept that repair is not failure but civic rhythm.

sections.heading: Food, clothing, and housing
content: Food culture is preservation culture. Salt fish, smoked roots, fermented grain, pickled reef vegetables, fungal breads, pressure-dried kelp, hard travel cheese, spice-sealed stews, and temple-stamped emergency cakes are common. The wealthy eat fresh fruit year-round because they can buy cooling charms and sealed transit; the poor eat what survives humidity.

Clothing is layered for wet heat, sudden storm, mud, insect pressure, and transit safety. Reef settlements favor quick-drying wraps and shell clasps. Caverns favor treated wool, leather, brass fasteners, and lamp-reflective trim. Cities mix formal silhouettes with practical ventilation. Travelers carry spare socks, waxed bags, salt packets, fever charms, and a written local-time conversion if they expect to cross longitude bands.

Housing is elevated, ventilated, limewashed, drained, and repairable. Roofs are steep where rain hits hard, flat only where they are inspected often. Marsh homes stand on raised walks. Reef homes use waterlocks. Cavern homes use condensation gutters. Treetop homes flex in wind. Rich houses may hide divine wards in beautiful plaster, but even poor homes keep a dry shelf for documents.

sections.heading: Education and childhood
content: Children learn sky, tide, rot, and route safety as basic literacy. A child may learn the four alignment axes before formal grammar because courts, temples, and guilds use them. They learn which monster names are literal and which are warnings. They learn that the big moon is not alone, that bridges need scraping, that a pretty cyan leak is not a toy, and that a god can be both imprisoned and dangerous.

sections.heading: 10. Death, Resurrection, and the Ledger
content: Death in Belavadös is active. The death god maintains a design, a sequence, and a ledger for every living creature. Every soul has an appointed moment written into reality. Whenever someone escapes that fate through luck, magic, prophecy, intervention, or coincidence, the design fractures. The god of death responds not as a passive judge but as a force that hunts correction.

Unconsciousness is not merely blood loss. Reaching the edge of death means the ledger has noticed the soul personally. Candles gutter, clocks stutter, rain may begin, mirrors may crack, animals may panic, and nearby witnesses may hear distant funeral bells. A failed death save is death tightening its grasp; a success is not triumph but theft.

sections.heading: Resurrection as cosmic debt
content: Resurrection magic exists, but it is not a clean reset. It may save a beloved life while moving pressure elsewhere. It may attract ledger-auditors, corpse rumors, omen animals, dream summons, or divine correction. Temples record resurrections as public spiritual events because an escaped death can change more than one person's fate.
A natural recovery can still leave a soul marked by cold memories, grave dreams, or a new fear of mirrors.
A resurrection may require witnesses, debt payment, a vow, a journey, a returned name, or a bargain with a hostile ledger.
Undead are not all the same: some are curses, some are debts, some are grief, some are legal mistakes, and some are deliberate resistance.
Necromancy is judged by context: funeral preservation, battlefield abuse, ancestral consultation, corpse labor, and resurrection theft are not treated equally.
Death festivals are part mourning, part audit, part appeasement, and part defiance.

sections.heading: Funeral culture
content: Funerals vary by biome. Reef funerals may release weighted lanterns into tide roads. Cavern funerals carve names into condensation stone. Farming villages bake memory bread and distribute it before rot can claim the grain. Treetop families hang bells where the wind can speak. Cities file death certificates with temple, court, and transit office because an unresolved death can close roads, inheritances, and magical permissions.

sections.heading: 11. Creatures, Ruins, and Monster Signs
content: Belavadös treats monsters as ecological and social facts. A monster may be a citizen, a plague, a holy sign, a market hazard, a faction asset, a weather metaphor, a food-chain pressure, a criminal partner, a legal category, or a reason a road was never built straight. outside-rule creature material is used as a bestiary language, but each creature is translated into Belavadös weather, gods, transit, death, and ichor logic.

sections.heading: Monster Words Used as Ecology, Weather, and Map Terms
Ruins, undercities, and buried works
content: Deep ruins in Belavadös are not empty mazes waiting for heroes. They are failed infrastructure, buried temples, prison-adjacent service tunnels, drowned archives, collapsed rail works, fungal cities, abandoned noble laboratories, old monster lairs, refuge networks, and places where weather can no longer leave. A good ruin has supply logic, waste routes, air, water, silence, old maps, new occupants, and at least one faction that wants the truth delayed.

Undercities matter because warm wet worlds build downward as often as upward. Mountain provinces carry deep cavern settlement networks. Coastal cities hide old flood levels beneath new markets. Dead stations become smuggler roads. Tombs become fungus farms. Dwarves, drow, tieflings, shadow peoples, miners, pressure engineers, and all those who prefer stone to sky make underlayers into real neighborhoods rather than background darkness.

sections.heading: Wilderness travel
content: Wilderness travel uses free movement, negotiation, ruin crawls, guerrilla routes, survival pressure, political encounter, and monster ecology. A lost-world island may preserve older beasts. A canyon may use rope and pulley law. A rainforest ruin may be more alive than abandoned. A reef may be an open-air ruin that floods twice a day. Every path should ask: who maintains it, what season breaks it, what creature reads it better than people do, and which faction profits if travelers vanish?

sections.heading: Monster Signs Before Blades Are Drawn
12. Factions, Law, Economy, and Quiet Living
content: Factions are living Belavadös powers: offices, cults, orders, syndicates, institutes, courts, machine-priesthoods, and public-service bodies. They attach themselves to routes, permits, settlement danger, province government, resident peoples, and access to ichor. A job becomes public when transit, rumor, paperwork, and witness culture make secrecy too expensive.

sections.heading: Settlement Scale and Everyday Population Feel
Legal crime and public violence
content: Some provinces recognize forms of registered violence, salvage rights, prize shares, cleanup bonds, target classes, collateral declarations, and witness fees. This does not make crime safe; it makes it bureaucratic. A rogue may need better paperwork than a paladin. A killing may be illegal in one district, taxable in another, and spiritually catastrophic in both.

sections.heading: Economy of daily work
content: Belavadös economies are based on food preservation, route maintenance, ichor licensing, repair labor, weather prediction, transit access, monster-response contracts, temple services, document drying, salvage law, and faction patronage. The most important workers are often not glamorous: bridge scrapers, roof menders, tide clerks, apothecaries, condenser cleaners, route translators, corpse registrars, signal operators, waterlock attendants, and public cooks.

sections.heading: Quiet living
content: Not everyone is an adventurer. Most lives are made of water collection, roof repair, family meals, transport fares, gossip, worship, work shifts, market bargaining, seasonal dread, and small pleasures. Quiet people know which fungus is edible, which clerk is kind, which road floods, which station clock lies, which faction recruiter smiles too much, and which constellation makes their grandmother whisper. The chronicle world feels large when ordinary people have reasons to live that are not simply waiting for heroes.

sections.heading: 13. Festivals, Constellations, and Seasonal Rhythm
content: Belavadös festivals follow the overlap of month theme, constellation witness, tide state, agricultural need, faction interest, and local disaster memory. A holiday is never only decorative. It opens markets, closes roads, suspends debts, permits masks, launches pilgrimages, changes patrol levels, alters transport loads, and tells ordinary people what danger society has agreed to notice.

sections.heading: Seasonal Calendar of Belavadös
content: Constellation holidays are civic instruments. Bastveig's Tidehook closes reef gates for pilgrim tides. Ishtanora's Hearthdrum opens village storehouses and harvest kitchens. Enkirael's Warfire legalizes certain contests of arms while making unsanctioned duels easier to prosecute. Nephthysra's Mirror turns reconciliation into public art, while Freyseth's Mask blesses disguises, confessions, and threshold bargains. Nefarokir's month is feared because funeral ledgers, death debts, and resurrection petitions are audited together.

sections.heading: 14. Journey Cues, Hazard Clocks, and Ordinary Days
content: Journeys in Belavadös are shaped by weather signs, local law, transit delays, monster movement, public mood, and the quiet labor of people who keep roofs, ferries, bridges, lamps, ledgers, and bodies working.

sections.heading: Dry Belts, Highlands, and Skyship Routes
15. References and Sources
content: The guide above keeps outside names and source notes out of the lived record. The references below remain here for source tracking, climate comparison, creature vocabulary, encounter structure, and cartographic provenance.
