full_extract.source_file: The Design of Death in Belavadös.docx
paragraphs: The Design of Death in Belavadös

In most Dungeons & Dragons campaigns, death is a temporary inconvenience disguised as tragedy. Characters fall unconscious, allies rush forward with Healing Word, a potion, or Spare the Dying, and the party continues onward. Even when someone truly dies, resurrection magic often transforms death into a logistical problem rather than a spiritual horror. In Belavadös, that changes completely. Death is no longer passive. It is no longer a simple mechanic sitting quietly behind the dice. Death is an active cosmic force. It hunts. It remembers. It corrects mistakes.

In this world, the god of death maintains a design, a sequence, and a ledger that governs every living creature. Every soul has an appointed moment of death written into reality itself. Whenever someone escapes that fate through luck, prophecy, magic, intervention, or coincidence, the design fractures. The god of death responds by pursuing the survivors until balance is restored. This transforms the tone of the campaign from heroic fantasy into supernatural dread. You should stop thinking about hit points as abstract combat resources and start thinking about survival as something fragile and temporary.

To make this concept work inside Dungeons & Dragons 5e, death saving throws become narrative events instead of silent dice rolls. Every failed death save should feel like death physically reaching toward your character. Every success should feel temporary and unnatural. Rather than quietly marking successes and failures on paper, I will describe the experience in vivid sensory detail. A failed death save might feel like icy water filling your lungs, invisible hands pulling your soul downward, distant funeral bells echoing through darkness, flickering visions of graves, or whispers from unseen entities. A successful death save will not feel triumphant. It will feel stolen. Your character survives something they were never supposed to survive.

The philosophy behind unconsciousness changes as well. In standard 5e, reaching zero hit points usually means a character is bleeding out. In this setting, reaching zero hit points means the god of death has noticed your character personally. The moment you drop to zero, reality begins bending around you. Candles extinguish. Clocks stop ticking. Animals panic. Mirrors crack. Rain begins suddenly. Small environmental omens reinforce that death is not simply waiting for three failed saves. Death is already in the room.

Death saving throws themselves represent your soul resisting the claim of the death god. A success represents your soul dragging itself back into your body. A failure represents death tightening its grasp. Rolling a natural 1 becomes terrifying because your character briefly crosses into the realm of the dead and returns with fragmented memories of it. Rolling a natural 20 is deeply unsettling rather than heroic. Instead of simply regaining 1 hit point, your character violently awakens with visions of future deaths, prophetic hallucinations, or impossible knowledge they were never meant to possess.

One of the most important themes of Belavadös is inevitability. Death cannot truly be defeated. It can only be delayed, redirected, or bargained with. There are only two known ways to escape the design for any meaningful amount of time. The first is murder. By intentionally killing another person, a character steals the remaining years from the victim’s destined lifespan. The second is temporary death followed by resurrection. A character who genuinely dies and is revived becomes difficult for the death god to track because their name briefly leaves the cosmic ledger before being rewritten.

The murder mechanic is intentionally mysterious. I will never reduce it to a visible countdown or numerical timer. Stolen years function more like metaphysical momentum. A murderer becomes harder for death to claim because another life has been substituted into the design. The victim effectively takes the killer’s place in the sequence. This creates horrifying moral tension throughout the campaign. Good aligned characters may be forced to confront the possibility that survival requires evil. Cowards may become killers. Noble characters may choose sacrifice instead of stealing innocent years. Some may rationalize murdering criminals, tyrants, or dying enemies. Others may spiral into paranoia and predation.

Mechanically, I may track this through something called borrowed years. Whenever a character intentionally kills an intelligent creature as part of a conscious attempt to escape death, I secretly determine how much protection was gained based on the victim’s remaining lifespan and importance within the design. During this protected period, death cannot directly target that character through supernatural accidents or unavoidable omens. However, the psychological burden grows heavier.

Characters carrying stolen years begin deteriorating emotionally and spiritually. They suffer recurring dreams from the victim’s perspective. They hear the dead person’s voice in crowded rooms. Their reflection occasionally resembles the victim. Animals react with fear or aggression around them. Clerics sense spiritual contamination. Resurrection magic cast upon them may behave unpredictably. This ensures that murder never becomes a clean optimization strategy. Extending life through violence leaves visible scars on the soul.

The second survival method, dying and being revived, preserves hope without removing fear. In this setting, resurrection magic does not defeat death. It only confuses the design temporarily. When a creature dies and returns to life, the death god loses track of the soul for a limited time because the soul crossed the boundary correctly before returning. This creates an important distinction between ordinary healing and true resurrection.

Healing magic does not protect against the design. Healing Word, Cure Wounds, and potions restore the body, but they do not erase the fact that the soul was marked for collection. Revivify, Raise Dead, Resurrection, and similar spells genuinely interrupt the cosmic sequence. Low level healing is no longer enough to escape consequences. Survival requires confronting death directly.

Revivify becomes especially significant because it resembles magical resuscitation. The character truly dies for a brief moment before returning. During that instant, they glimpse the realm of the death god. Every revived character returns changed. Perhaps their body temperature remains unnaturally cold forever. Perhaps mirrors stop reflecting them properly. Maybe food tastes like ash. Maybe they hear whispers whenever they are alone. Resurrection leaves permanent marks.

I may represent these through marks of return. Every resurrection leaves behind a supernatural alteration chosen to reinforce the horror and atmosphere of the setting. One character may lose the ability to sleep naturally. Another may bleed black instead of red. Another might attract ghosts. Another may permanently smell faintly of grave dirt after rainfall. These changes are not meant to heavily punish players mechanically. Their purpose is narrative dread and immersion.

Death itself behaves intelligently and creatively. The environment becomes hostile in subtle escalating ways. At first, accidents seem coincidental. A chandelier sways overhead. A horse panics unexpectedly. Oil spills across stone floors. A bridge creaks ominously. Over time, the pattern becomes undeniable. Reality itself is attempting to complete the design.

These sequences are never meant to feel unfair. The horror comes from inevitability and tension rather than arbitrary punishment. There will always be clues beforehand and opportunities to intervene. A tavern fire begins with smoke, nervous servants, and crackling beams long before collapse occurs. A wagon accident begins with frightened horses and damaged wheels. You will recognize danger approaching even if you cannot fully predict how events will unfold.

Environmental hazards are layered together deliberately. A leaking lantern alone is not frightening. A leaking lantern beside spilled alcohol near frightened horses during a thunderstorm while an exhausted blacksmith works nearby becomes terrifying. You should begin examining your surroundings constantly. Ordinary environments become sources of paranoia.

Combat changes dramatically under this system as well. Battles stop being isolated tactical encounters and instead become opportunities for death itself to interfere. A fighter reduced to zero hit points may suddenly notice the battlefield turning against them. Broken pillars collapse. Loose arrows ignite spilled oil. A dying enemy accidentally triggers a trap. The god of death manipulates probability itself.

Resurrection magic across the world carries a darker reputation. Priests no longer treat resurrection casually. Temples fear repeated revivals because they attract the attention of the death god. Clerics understand that every resurrection creates imbalance. Some faiths outlaw resurrection entirely except under extreme circumstances. Others demand terrible sacrifices in exchange.

Diamonds used for resurrection magic become symbolically important in this setting. They may be crystallized fragments of souls that resisted death long ago. Each resurrection literally burns spiritual essence to obscure a soul from the design temporarily. Material spell components stop feeling transactional and begin carrying thematic weight.

NPCs who escaped death become deeply unsettling figures throughout the campaign. You may encounter a man who murdered dozens to extend his lifespan yet still sees death approaching everywhere. You may meet an old queen resurrected six times whose body slowly decays despite remaining alive. You may discover assassins hired specifically to kill marked individuals before the design escalates into larger catastrophes.

Visions are another major roleplaying element. Characters marked by death occasionally receive prophetic glimpses of future fatalities. These visions are fragmented, symbolic, and incomplete. A character may see shattered stained glass, hear children screaming, and smell smoke days before a cathedral collapse. Another may glimpse blood floating in bathwater before a noble’s murder. These visions create tension because disaster is coming even when its meaning remains unclear.

The order of death also matters. After surviving a catastrophe, characters may realize the design is pursuing them in sequence. Each death changes who is next. Every resurrection, sacrifice, and murder reshapes the order. The party may begin obsessively tracking the sequence themselves. Entire sessions may revolve around preventing disasters before they occur.

This naturally encourages strong roleplay because every character reacts differently to mortality. One may become recklessly nihilistic. Another may become deeply religious. Another may pursue immortality through forbidden magic. Another may emotionally isolate themselves to avoid hurting others when death eventually arrives.
At the center of the campaign lies one question. What are people willing to do to survive?

That question becomes even more disturbing when innocent people become endangered by the design. If death cannot reach its target directly, collateral damage escalates. Buildings collapse. Ships sink. Fires spread through crowded districts. The party gradually realizes their continued survival threatens everyone around them.

This creates opportunities for moral horror. A character protected by stolen years may remain temporarily safe while everyone nearby suffers escalating danger. Communities may fear those who have been resurrected. Entire towns may exile marked individuals. Some groups may argue that one person should willingly die to stop the cycle.

Exhaustion and trauma may reinforce the emotional cost of cheating death. Repeated resurrections strain the spirit. Repeated survival leaves psychological scars. Characters may become sleepless, detached, paranoid, or emotionally numb from constantly standing at the edge of mortality.

Death omens appear more frequently around marked characters. Ravens gather nearby. Milk spoils instantly. Insects swarm unnaturally. Strangers avoid eye contact without understanding why. Divination magic becomes distorted in subtle ways.

The death god itself remains mostly unseen. The less directly understood it is, the more frightening it becomes. It is not a traditional villain giving speeches or issuing threats. It behaves more like a cosmic law with intelligence behind it. It does not hate mortals. It simply restores balance.

Occasionally, however, its agents may appear. Pale masked figures, grave wardens, psychopomps, or silent observers may arrive near disasters or resurrection sites. Sometimes they simply watch. Sometimes they warn against further resistance. Sometimes they quietly collect souls after tragedy strikes.

Death is also patient. If the party successfully avoids one attempt, the pressure may vanish temporarily. Life appears normal again. Tension fades. Weeks later, another elaborate chain of events begins unexpectedly. This unpredictability keeps the atmosphere from becoming repetitive.

The structure of the campaign supports investigation based storytelling beautifully. The party may uncover records of previous death cycles. Entire villages may have vanished centuries ago after someone cheated death repeatedly. Ancient kings may have massacred thousands to extend their reigns. Hidden cults may worship the death god by helping restore the proper order.

Even undead creatures fit naturally into this cosmology. Ghosts are souls that escaped collection improperly. Revenants are beings intentionally allowed to persist until an imbalance is corrected. Liches represent ultimate rebellion against the design. Vampires survive by stealing life essence because they permanently exist outside the natural cycle.

The atmosphere of the campaign constantly emphasizes fragility. I will describe unstable architecture, old ropes, cracked glass, slippery stones, flickering flames, rusted chains, and exhausted workers with deliberate detail. Ordinary objects become threatening because the environment itself can become part of the design.

At the same time, moments of humanity become even more important. Quiet campfire conversations matter because survival is uncertain. Friendships deepen because nobody expects longevity. Romance becomes tragic because every future feels fragile.

Survivor’s guilt becomes unavoidable for many characters. Anyone who escapes through murder or resurrection eventually questions whether they deserved to survive. Clerics may struggle with their faith after reviving companions repeatedly. Paladins may break their oaths. Rogues may rationalize atrocities. Even successful survival leaves emotional consequences.

Prophecy also becomes deeply unsettling. Seers and oracles are feared because they glimpse fragments of the design constantly. Some blind themselves to avoid seeing death everywhere they look. Others profit by selling incomplete warnings. False prophecies become especially dangerous because misunderstanding the design often accelerates disaster instead of preventing it.

During major death sequences, pacing changes dramatically. Narration slows. Positioning matters. Every sound and movement becomes important. A simple tavern scene can become terrifying once every object in the room suddenly feels dangerous.

Mechanically, I want to avoid overcomplicating the system. The power of Belavadös comes primarily from atmosphere, roleplay, and tension. Standard 5e mechanics already support much of this naturally. Only minor adjustments are necessary.

One possible adjustment is preventing failed death saves from resetting immediately through ordinary healing. In standard 5e, any healing clears failed saves completely. In Belavadös, failed saves may linger until a long rest because your soul was still touched by death. This makes repeated knockdowns increasingly dangerous.

I may also track a hidden pressure system for each character. Escaping fatal events, surviving prophecies, using resurrection magic, or stealing years increases the pressure surrounding that character. The higher it grows, the more aggressively reality attempts correction. You will never know the exact number, only the escalating consequences.

Most importantly, Belavadös depends on everyone embracing the tone together. Death is omnipresent, psychologically oppressive, and morally corrosive. Survival always carries a cost. Fear, tension, investigation, and character drama are central to the experience.
Every combat becomes meaningful. Every resurrection becomes emotionally significant. Every death save becomes terrifying.

By treating death as an intelligent cosmic force instead of a simple mechanical state, the campaign transforms into something uniquely haunting. The question eventually stops being whether your characters can survive. The real question becomes what survival is worth.
In the end, the true horror of this setting is not dying. The true horror is discovering what people become when death refuses to let them go.

Death itself behaves intelligently and creatively. The environment becomes hostile in subtle escalating ways. At first, accidents seem coincidental. A chandelier sways overhead. A horse panics unexpectedly. Oil spills across stone floors. A bridge creaks ominously. Over time, the pattern becomes undeniable. Reality itself is attempting to complete the design.

These sequences are never meant to feel unfair. The horror comes from inevitability and tension rather than arbitrary punishment. There will always be clues beforehand and opportunities to intervene. A tavern fire begins with smoke, nervous servants, and crackling beams long before collapse occurs. A wagon accident begins with frightened horses and damaged wheels. You will recognize danger approaching even if you cannot fully predict how events will unfold.

Environmental hazards are layered together deliberately. A leaking lantern alone is not frightening. A leaking lantern beside spilled alcohol near frightened horses during a thunderstorm while an exhausted blacksmith works nearby becomes terrifying. You should begin examining your surroundings constantly. Ordinary environments become sources of paranoia.

Combat changes dramatically under this system as well. Battles stop being isolated tactical encounters and instead become opportunities for death itself to interfere. A fighter reduced to zero hit points may suddenly notice the battlefield turning against them. Broken pillars collapse. Loose arrows ignite spilled oil. A dying enemy accidentally triggers a trap. The god of death manipulates probability itself.

Resurrection magic across the world carries a darker reputation. Priests no longer treat resurrection casually. Temples fear repeated revivals because they attract the attention of the death god. Clerics understand that every resurrection creates imbalance. Some faiths outlaw resurrection entirely except under extreme circumstances. Others demand terrible sacrifices in exchange.

Diamonds used for resurrection magic become symbolically important in this setting. They may be crystallized fragments of souls that resisted death long ago. Each resurrection literally burns spiritual essence to obscure a soul from the design temporarily. Material spell components stop feeling transactional and begin carrying thematic weight.

NPCs who escaped death become deeply unsettling figures throughout the campaign. You may encounter a man who murdered dozens to extend his lifespan yet still sees death approaching everywhere. You may meet an old queen resurrected six times whose body slowly decays despite remaining alive. You may discover assassins hired specifically to kill marked individuals before the design escalates into larger catastrophes.

Visions are another major roleplaying element. Characters marked by death occasionally receive prophetic glimpses of future fatalities. These visions are fragmented, symbolic, and incomplete. A character may see shattered stained glass, hear children screaming, and smell smoke days before a cathedral collapse. Another may glimpse blood floating in bathwater before a noble’s murder. These visions create tension because disaster is coming even when its meaning remains unclear.

The order of death also matters. After surviving a catastrophe, characters may realize the design is pursuing them in sequence. Each death changes who is next. Every resurrection, sacrifice, and murder reshapes the order. The party may begin obsessively tracking the sequence themselves. Entire sessions may revolve around preventing disasters before they occur.

This naturally encourages strong roleplay because every character reacts differently to mortality. One may become recklessly nihilistic. Another may become deeply religious. Another may pursue immortality through forbidden magic. Another may emotionally isolate themselves to avoid hurting others when death eventually arrives.
At the center of the campaign lies one question. What are people willing to do to survive?

That question becomes even more disturbing when innocent people become endangered by the design. If death cannot reach its target directly, collateral damage escalates. Buildings collapse. Ships sink. Fires spread through crowded districts. The party gradually realizes their continued survival threatens everyone around them.

This creates opportunities for moral horror. A character protected by stolen years may remain temporarily safe while everyone nearby suffers escalating danger. Communities may fear those who have been resurrected. Entire towns may exile marked individuals. Some groups may argue that one person should willingly die to stop the cycle.

Exhaustion and trauma may reinforce the emotional cost of cheating death. Repeated resurrections strain the spirit. Repeated survival leaves psychological scars. Characters may become sleepless, detached, paranoid, or emotionally numb from constantly standing at the edge of mortality.

Death omens appear more frequently around marked characters. Ravens gather nearby. Milk spoils instantly. Insects swarm unnaturally. Strangers avoid eye contact without understanding why. Divination magic becomes distorted in subtle ways.

The death god itself remains mostly unseen. The less directly understood it is, the more frightening it becomes. It is not a traditional villain giving speeches or issuing threats. It behaves more like a cosmic law with intelligence behind it. It does not hate mortals. It simply restores balance.

Occasionally, however, its agents may appear. Pale masked figures, grave wardens, psychopomps, or silent observers may arrive near disasters or resurrection sites. Sometimes they simply watch. Sometimes they warn against further resistance. Sometimes they quietly collect souls after tragedy strikes.

Death is also patient. If the party successfully avoids one attempt, the pressure may vanish temporarily. Life appears normal again. Tension fades. Weeks later, another elaborate chain of events begins unexpectedly. This unpredictability keeps the atmosphere from becoming repetitive.

The structure of the campaign supports investigation based storytelling beautifully. The party may uncover records of previous death cycles. Entire villages may have vanished centuries ago after someone cheated death repeatedly. Ancient kings may have massacred thousands to extend their reigns. Hidden cults may worship the death god by helping restore the proper order.

Even undead creatures fit naturally into this cosmology. Ghosts are souls that escaped collection improperly. Revenants are beings intentionally allowed to persist until an imbalance is corrected. Liches represent ultimate rebellion against the design. Vampires survive by stealing life essence because they permanently exist outside the natural cycle.

The atmosphere of the campaign constantly emphasizes fragility. I will describe unstable architecture, old ropes, cracked glass, slippery stones, flickering flames, rusted chains, and exhausted workers with deliberate detail. Ordinary objects become threatening because the environment itself can become part of the design.

At the same time, moments of humanity become even more important. Quiet campfire conversations matter because survival is uncertain. Friendships deepen because nobody expects longevity. Romance becomes tragic because every future feels fragile.

Survivor’s guilt becomes unavoidable for many characters. Anyone who escapes through murder or resurrection eventually questions whether they deserved to survive. Clerics may struggle with their faith after reviving companions repeatedly. Paladins may break their oaths. Rogues may rationalize atrocities. Even successful survival leaves emotional consequences.

Prophecy also becomes deeply unsettling. Seers and oracles are feared because they glimpse fragments of the design constantly. Some blind themselves to avoid seeing death everywhere they look. Others profit by selling incomplete warnings. False prophecies become especially dangerous because misunderstanding the design often accelerates disaster instead of preventing it.

During major death sequences, pacing changes dramatically. Narration slows. Positioning matters. Every sound and movement becomes important. A simple tavern scene can become terrifying once every object in the room suddenly feels dangerous.

Mechanically, I want to avoid overcomplicating the system. The power of Belavadös comes primarily from atmosphere, roleplay, and tension. Standard 5e mechanics already support much of this naturally. Only minor adjustments are necessary.

One possible adjustment is preventing failed death saves from resetting immediately through ordinary healing. In standard 5e, any healing clears failed saves completely. In Belavadös, failed saves may linger until a long rest because your soul was still touched by death. This makes repeated knockdowns increasingly dangerous.

I may also track a hidden pressure system for each character. Escaping fatal events, surviving prophecies, using resurrection magic, or stealing years increases the pressure surrounding that character. The higher it grows, the more aggressively reality attempts correction. You will never know the exact number, only the escalating consequences.

Most importantly, Belavadös depends on everyone embracing the tone together. Death is omnipresent, psychologically oppressive, and morally corrosive. Survival always carries a cost. Fear, tension, investigation, and character drama are central to the experience.
Every combat becomes meaningful. Every resurrection becomes emotionally significant. Every death save becomes terrifying.

By treating death as an intelligent cosmic force instead of a simple mechanical state, the campaign transforms into something uniquely haunting. The question eventually stops being whether your characters can survive. The real question becomes what survival is worth.
In the end, the true horror of this setting is not dying. The true horror is discovering what people become when death refuses to let them go.

manifest.title: Belavadös ATA Transit System
manifest.description: Realmwide public transit rebuilt from the final four-compendium province and settlement placement.
manifest.railOceanRule: Rail stays on land corridors, tunnels, bridges, river spans, lake spans, and coastal causeways; vast open ocean crossings are not rail service.

timeConversionRules.offsetMethod: Nearest whole-hour longitude band: offsetHours = round(longitude / 15), clamped from BMT-12 to BMT+12.
timeConversionRules.latitudeUse: Latitude is recorded on every settlement certificate and confirms the settlement coordinate and hemisphere; the public hour offset is assigned by longitude so route clocks stay consistent.
timeConversionRules.localClockRule: Every passenger-facing arrival, release, and transfer time is posted in the local time of the settlement where that event happens.
timeConversionRules.originDepartureRule: Published departures are origin-terminal local time. Once the vehicle is in motion, every later stop is converted from absolute elapsed travel time into that stop’s local clock.
timeConversionRules.timeZoneCrossingRule: Eastbound clock crossings move the displayed local clock ahead; westbound clock crossings move it behind. Date labels may move forward or backward when the clock crosses midnight.
timeConversionRules.portalRule: Portal crossings obey the same settlement-local clock ledger. A portal can create a large visible clock jump because the traveler changes longitude almost at once, even when the controlled crossing itself is short.
timeConversionRules.wednesdayRule: Wednesday schedules keep their slower movement and added ichor checks, then receive the same local settlement time conversion.

paragraphs: Belavadös Night Sky
Celestial reference for sky time, moons, wandering worlds, nebula fields, distant stars, sky-lights, and constellations
The Hungry Gods Await
Index
1. Guide and sky-time rules
2. Sky setting and Star-River
3. Celestial inventory
4. Constellations
5. Two moons in the Belavadös sky
6. Worlds, regions, and comet
7. Distant stars and sky-lights of Belavadös
8. Representative night
9. Source and method notes
1. Guide and sky-time rules
Naming and replacement rules used in this document
• The bright band crossing the sky is called the Star-River of Belavadös.
• The observing landscape is described as the Great River Valley and its desert-edge skyfields.
• The twelve wandering planets and two moons use the supplied invented names and coordinates.
• The sky analysis keeps historical-style latitude, precession, seasonality, and horizon logic, but is written as Belavadös sky lore rather than a modern archaeological report.
Coordinate system used

The sky is described with right ascension and declination. These coordinates function like celestial longitude and latitude. Apparent magnitude uses lower numbers for brighter objects, with negative values being especially bright. Planet and moon distances use AU or kilometers; stellar distances use light-years.
Earth and Belavadös sky time

Use Earth dates and Earth time first for players, session schedules, travel timing, event boards, and deadlines. Use Belavadös dates second for lore records, temple calendars, journals, festivals, and immersion. A Belavadös astronomical year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days long, and those solar days are distributed evenly across the Earth year for table play.

For sky calculations, use solar progress rather than the named civil date. The civil calendar still has 330 named dates arranged as eleven 30-date months, while the 0.15 solar-day correction is spread through the year as a tiny clock drift. There is no bonus day or frozen end-period for moons, planets, tides, omens, or the Star-River.
Sky conversion formula
1. daysInEarthYear = 365, or 366 in a leap year.
2. earthProgress = (Earth day-of-year - 1 + fractionOfEarthDay) / daysInEarthYear.
3. belSolarDayProgress = earthProgress x 330.15. Use this value for moon phases, planetary positions, tides, constellations, seasons, and sky omens.
4. belCivilDateProgress = earthProgress x 330. Use this value only for the named Belavadös month and date.
5. Belavadös clock time may use the fractional part of belSolarDayProgress x 24.
Player-facing observing log format
Write sky events Earth-first, then Belavadös-second: Earth Month Day, Year, local time with UTC label / Belavadös month date, weekday, Belavadös clock, solar-day progress, moon phase, and sky note.

Settlement and province sky notes may include the settlement UTC when the observing site differs from the province primary UTC. Province summaries should show only one or two Earth-style UTC labels, while exact settlement exports can store the UTC chosen by longitude.
Belavadös month cycle for sky records

These month names are used for date labels only. A moon, wandering world, tide, season, or sky omen should still be calculated from belSolarDayProgress so the sky remains smooth across the full Earth year.
2. Sky setting and Star-River
Historical-style sky setting
The analysis assumes a view from approximately 30° N latitude. At 30° N, stars above about +60° declination are circumpolar, while stars below about -60° declination never rise.

The sky looks dark, dense, and sharply structured. With no electric skyglow, the Star-River of Belavadös would have been a major visible feature rather than a faint haze. Bright planets, bright stars, both moons, and future named sky patterns can serve as seasonal markers, navigation guides, calendar anchors, and story-bearing landmarks.
The Star-River of Belavadös

The Star-River of Belavadös is the luminous band of unresolved stars and dark rifts crossing the night sky. In summer evenings, it would stretch through the southern gate-and-serpent sectors and climb toward the northern seasonal markers. In winter evenings, it would run near the Bronze Bull region, becoming paler but still visible under dry, dark conditions.

From desert-edge skyfields, the Star-River would not have appeared as a smooth strip. It would have looked mottled, braided, and broken by dark channels. The brightest warm-season section would have been low-to-mid in the southern sky; the higher northern section would have served as a nightly path for visual navigation.
Nebula fields of Belavadös
Each nebula uses the same field layout for generator use: coordinate anchor, distance/span, type, dominant colors, layer structure, and texture/components.
Âhufej — Minotaur Labyrinth of Anubaldir
Dus‘idu — Silkborn Web of Thoryn-Rahek
Ềdizfu — Dragonborn Dominion of Valkhamesh
Juçdimx — Crossroads Mask of Freyseth
Jadd-Jisud — Wechselkind Crown of Setrimir
Horundar — Sahuagin Deep Gate of Bastveig
Wougen — Luma Mirror of Nephthysra
Ŝiowoei — Dragonborn Dominion outer spiral
3. Celestial inventory
This inventory separates fixed stars, upper-atmosphere light, moons, worlds, regions, nebula fields, and the blank constellation placeholder so each part of the sky reference has one clear home.
4. Constellations

These are the sky-names used when the Gods still walked openly across Belavadös, before their prisons, before public ichor engines, before rail bells, portal halls, and industrial skyports taught cities to trust machines more than stars. The names are the names carved into tide stairs, burial ledgers, cairn roads, hearth beams, watchtower lintels, reef shrines, and desert-edge observatories.
Each figure keeps its fixed place in the sky. The names belong to Belavadös. The coordinates preserve the star-path for sky maps, generators, omen records, and night watches.
4.1. How skykeepers read the fixed heavens

Belavadös skykeepers use right ascension and declination as the fixed grid of the upper world. Right ascension runs from 0h to 24h around the sky. Declination rises north or south of the sky-equator. Magnitude records visible brightness; the smaller the number, the stronger the light.

Seasonal movement follows the 330.15 day Belavadös solar year. Civil dates still belong to the eleven named months, but the sky obeys solar progress. Moon phases, tides, wandering worlds, Star-River omens, and constellation seasons move smoothly across the whole year.

The old horizon rule is simple enough for any watchtower: at about 30 degrees north, lights above about +60 degrees stay near the northern sky and lights below about -60 degrees never rise. Other latitudes shift the height of the figures without moving the figures themselves.
Sky-record months
4.2. Constellation register
4.3. Seasonal and hemispheric visibility
Northern and southern visibility depends on latitude and season. East-west behavior describes how the pattern rises, crosses the meridian, sets, or circles the northern sky during the night.
4.4. Star layouts and coordinate anchors

The following tables preserve the fixed coordinates of each light and sky waypoint. Names are Belavadös names. RA and Dec are the placement anchors used by sky maps, temple charts, observatories, and generators.
Anubaldir's Labyrinth
Bastveig's Tidehook
Setrimir's Diadem
Thoryn-Rahek's Web
Enkirael's Warfire
Nephthysra's Mirror
Sokhivar's Lantern
Ishtanora's Hearthdrum
Freyseth's Mask
The Star-River
The Three Watches
The Spirit Lights
4.5. Skykeeper practice

Harbors, caravan wells, funeral roads, terrace farms, reef shrines, and high watchtowers all keep different portions of the same sky. Coastal settlements read Bastveig's Tidehook, Freyseth's Mask, the Star-River, and the two moons for water law. Mountain and inland roads favor Anubaldir's Labyrinth, Enkirael's Warfire, and Setrimir's Diadem. Hearth villages mark Ishtanora's Hearthdrum, while temple singers and roof watchers keep Sokhivar's Lantern.

The old rule remains unchanged: a constellation is a witness. A vow spoken beneath a named figure is never only private. The sky is a ledger, a road, a tide stair, a battlefield, a mirror, a hearth, and a warning. When the Gods were free, this was not metaphor. It was daily survival.
5. Two moons in the Belavadös sky

The lunar system is nested: the larger moon orbits the world, while the smaller moonlet orbits the larger moon and is carried along with it. This creates paired lunar calendars, small bead-like crossings, and a subtle secondary tidal pulse. For Earth sessions, both lunar positions are calculated from belSolarDayProgress, not from the civil month and date.
Lunar phase pacing for Earth sessions
Chandratecu-Seleneš phase = (belSolarDayProgress mod 19.20) / 19.20.
Mictlindra-Nannara phase = (belSolarDayProgress mod 2.02) / 2.02.
Use the resulting fraction as the phase position in the lunar cycle. This keeps both moons moving continuously across non-leap and leap Earth years.
Moon size and world-relative scale
System behavior
6. Worlds, regions, and comet

The worlds orbit their star upon a relatively flat shared plane known as the Celestial Road. Belavadös itself remains the 1.00 AU reference world with a 330.15 Belavadös-day astronomical year; player-facing dates distribute that year evenly across the Earth calendar.
Major worlds
Minor worlds
Minor worlds are rounded celestial bodies that share their orbital regions with numerous smaller bodies.
Celestial regions
Observed worlds
Orbital placement and visibility
Color and appearance
Eiršu'neth Comet

The Eiršu'neth Comet is a massive, long-period Vishtecu–Hyperu family comet distinguished by its unusually large icy nucleus, high mass, and stable yet dramatic inclined orbit through the outer Belavadös system. With a nucleus about 85 miles (137 km) wide—roughly 10–50 times larger than a typical comet core—and an estimated mass around 500 trillion tons (about 500× that of an average comet), it is one of the most visually and dynamically significant comets in its region. It follows a repeating 6.48 Belavadös-year orbit (≈ 2,139.37 Belavadös days), with a semi-major axis of ~3.48 AU, ranging from a perihelion of 2.08 AU to an aphelion of 4.87 AU. Its 18° inclination above the Celestial Road and carefully positioned crossing points make it a safe, non-impacting body despite its size, periodically producing a spectacular multi-month display as it passes through the inner reaches of its orbit.
7. Distant stars and sky-lights of Belavadös

The fixed sky entries are grouped by location and object type. Each table uses the same columns: number, name, type, distance, magnitude, color, RA, Dec, and role/visibility. No formation data is included in this section.
Northern storm-crested stars
High northern and mid-northern stars around RA 19h-22h; mostly blue-white, amber, and red-orange points.
Northern mirror, glass, and crown stars
Mid-northern stars around RA 12h-16h; mirror, glass, crown, paw, veil, and flare markers.
Northern labyrinth and cold-season hearth stars
Northern cold-season field around RA 04h-06h; horn, gate, hearth, veil, kidfire, and battlevale markers.
Northern polar, crown, and window stars
Far-northern and polar guide field from RA 23h through 01h, plus a high north-hook marker.
Northern web and high-trail stars
Northern web, strand, knot, companion, and blade markers around RA 08h-13h.
Equatorial line and frost stars
Near-equator and low-declination line field around RA 05h; blue-white anchors, frost points, edge markers, and brow lanterns.
Equatorial hearth and rim stars
Low-declination hearth, rim, beat, cord, and tail markers around RA 10h-12h.
Compact blue-white cluster-field stars
Tight northern cluster-field points around RA 03h45m; thread, pearl, spark, and glow markers.
Southern water and threshold stars
Southern water-linked lintel, pillar, threshold, ward, fang, pearl, well, and lantern markers around RA 16h-17h.
Southern mask and crossroads stars
Southern and low-southern eye, smile, mask, and road markers around RA 21h-22h.
Far-southern deep-sky cloud marker
A far-southern luminous cloud entry with a fixed RA/Dec anchor but non-stellar object type.
Upper-atmosphere sky-light labels
These labels refer to upper-atmosphere light rather than fixed stars. They use no RA/Dec because their appearance depends on magnetic latitude, solar activity, darkness, and weather.
8. Representative night

A representative high-era observing night can be generated by first calculating belSolarDayProgress from the Earth date and local observing time, then placing Chandratecu-Seleneš and Mictlindra-Nannara along their 19.20-day and 2.02-day cycles. A sample scene may place the paired lunar system near RA 06h 15m and Dec +18° to +19°, close to the northern cold-season field and high enough for easy viewing from 30° N.

When the bright inner planet Mardukesh-Huitra is favorably placed, it dominates the evening or dawn sky with pearl-white brilliance. Surixoch-Aresu appears copper-red and lower near twilight. The four ringed planets are not equally easy to interpret with the unaided eye, but under magnification their ring lore becomes central: Vishtecu-Hyperu shows a rose-gold hairline, Enlimitra a frosted silver span, Quetzal-Hermeshu a tilted green-bronze eye, and Varunatl-Kronu a white-ringed blue elongation.
9. Source and method notes

The astronomical logic in this document uses standard sky-coordinate concepts: right ascension, declination, apparent magnitude, latitude-dependent visibility, horizon limits, axial precession, and a 330.15 day Belavadös astronomical year distributed evenly across the Earth year for play. The values are intended for generators, lore notes, sky omens, transit boards, and table-facing observing logs.

No Earth star names are included. The document is intended as a lore-compatible sky reference for Belavadös and as a practical coordinate table for generators; the fixed stars are deliberately placed at remote background distances and several are faint enough to be only partially visible without unusually dark skies or magnification.
Reference ledger
• Belavadös sky-time framework: 330.15 day astronomical year, 330-date civil calendar, eleven named months, and Earth-first table play conversion.
• Belavadös celestial register: moons, wandering worlds, comet, celestial regions, nebula fields, distant stars, sky-light labels, and constellation coordinates.
• Sky-coordinate method: right ascension, declination, apparent magnitude, latitude-dependent visibility, horizon limits, and seasonal star movement.
• Lore basis: Age of Open Gods skykeeping, imprisoned-god pantheon memory, pre-industrial temple astronomy, tide law, road law, burial ledgers, and post-ichor infrastructure context.

rows: Foreground soot lanes (900 ly), dense emission nursery (1,380 ly), red-brown rear cloud (5,800 ly)

Dense newborn stellar nursery with glowing hydrogen chambers. Rose tones arise from ionized hydrogen, gold from embedded young stars illuminating dust grains, while smoke-violet regions form where cooler molecular gas mingles with shadowed dust curtains. Texture resembles folded velvet mixed with branching smoke channels. Numerous protostars, Bok globules, and accretion knots are embedded throughout.

rows: Silver strand foreground (1,100 ly), supernova shell (2,100 ly), violet mutation veil (6,200 ly)

Extremely filamentary remnant structure. Cyan and jade hues indicate oxygen-rich shock fronts while white regions mark compressed gas where multiple shock waves intersect. Texture appears as torn silk, braided tendrils, and lace-like membranes. Contains expanding ejecta sheets, ionized oxygen filaments, sulfur traces, and high-energy particle fronts.

rows: Foreground sparks (1,800 ly), storm sheet (4,200 ly), primary rift flower (5,600 ly), violet dust rear layer (7,900 ly)

Vast petal-shaped dark nebula carved through a glowing emission field. Crimson and magenta petals surround blue-black voids where dense molecular dust blocks starlight. Texture resembles layered flower petals made of smoke and velvet. Contains cold molecular clouds, active collapse zones, dark filaments, and bright ionization ridges outlining the rift edges.

rows: Front ash layer (2,000 ly), reflective dust basin (3,400 ly), curse smoke (5,100 ly), under-road shadow (10,300 ly)

A highly reflective dust field illuminated by nearby blue stars. Silver and pearl regions arise from light scattering by fine silicate particles. Texture resembles finished frost, drifting fog banks, and layered mirror-glass sheets. Contains reflective silicate dust, carbonaceous smoke clouds, and fragmented molecular lanes.

rows: Metal-blue shell (2,200 ly), green shell (4,800 ly), primary red-amber shell cluster (8,900 ly), lost-key echo layer (9,600 ly)

Collection of overlapping planetary-nebula remnants. Amber and red shells arise from hydrogen and nitrogen emissions, while charcoal gaps reveal exhausted central cavities. Texture appears as stacked bubbles, fractured onion skins, and cracked glass spheres. Components include dying stellar cores, expanding gas shells, metallic ion clouds, and dusty ejecta rings.

Texture resembles sea fog, frost plumes, and subcombined currents. Rich in volatile compounds, comet embryos, crystalline ice grains, and reflective dust sheets.

rows: Blue foreground haze (1,200 ly), star-forming core (2,850 ly), mirror sheet (3,600 ly), rose backwash (6,300 ly)

Massive molecular cloud actively producing stellar clusters. Green-gold regions arise from mixed oxygen and dust reflection, cream tones from warm embedded stars. rows: Temple saying: The sky is not decoration. It is the first map, the first calendar, the first witness, and the oldest court still looking down.

tables.caption_or_previous_text: The old horizon rule is simple enough for any watchtower: at about 30 degrees north, lights above about +60 degrees stay near the northern sky and lights below about -60 degrees never rise. Other latitudes shift the height of the figures without moving the figures themselves.
rows: Age of Open Gods: The oldest names are devotional, practical, and fearful. They belong to farmers reading harvest weather, sailors reading tide and reef, caravan guides reading desert night, burial clerks reading Nefarokir's ledger, and temple astronomers watching for the moods of hungry divine powers.

rows: Skykeeper reading: A maze of horn, stone, burden, and watchfire. Giants, minotaurs, cavern guides, and winter cattlefolk read this figure as the gate of endurance. In the Age of Open Gods, vows of strength were sworn under it before mountain crossings and before entering deep stone. At its height, Anubaldir was believed to weigh every road against the body that dared to walk it.

Central clustered light; heart of the winter labyrinth field.
Red-orange eye marker in the stone-and-horn field.
Northern horn point in the visible gate.
Bright western stone of the gate.
Gate-line marker in the winter labyrinth.
Lower gate-light; bright hinge of the labyrinth.

Skykeeper reading: A straight bright line near the celestial equator, remembered by fishers, reef-watchers, winter sailors, and children learning the first sky-paths. The three central lights are the hook, bait, and knot; the surrounding fires mark shoulders, brow, blade, and frost. It belongs to the sea long before engines, when tide, hunger, and weather decided whether a boat returned.

Red shoulder ember; its changing light is watched for winter omens.
Blue-white lower frost point; a dangerous oath-star in old winter rites.

Skykeeper reading: A turning diadem around the northern sky, prized by gate wardens, night travellers, watchtowers, and early makers of clockwork shrines. The highest point is the northward jewel. Before the prison forges, Setrimir was honored and feared as the thief of waking metal, and this pattern marked direction, order, and the knowledge mortals were not meant to hold.

Skykeeper reading: A broad high web of knot, strand, fang, pulse, drop, eye, ember, and blade. It is the sky of primordial bodies and old malformed life. Hunters used it to keep direction; plague-priests used it to mark mutation seasons; children were warned not to count every strand aloud, because Thoryn-Rahek remembers attention.

Brightest road-light in the high web.
Close paired light with Needle-Eye Ember.
Companion eye-test star near Opteran Eye; used in old winter oath readings.
Blade at the end of the high trail.

Skykeeper reading: A bright cold-season hearth surrounded by spear, shield, veil, and paired sparks. Warriors saw a campfire before a final battle; oathbreakers saw a tribunal; soldiers saw marching fires over winter fields. During the open reign of the Gods, captains waited for this pattern to rise before declaring a lawful campaign.
Winter evenings and early spring; high overhead at mid-northern latitudes.

Skykeeper reading: A tight hearth of rim, beat, cord, thread, pearl, shared spark, and brother-glow. It is the common sky-sign of villages, granaries, harvest dancing, and children counted safely indoors. Rural households treated its first clear rising as a promise that the hearth still belonged to the living.
Compact hearth cluster and smallfolk drum
Late autumn through winter evenings; low east in fall, high south by winter, west in early spring.

Late spring through summer evenings; low in the southern sky from mid-northern latitudes.

Skykeeper reading: The mottled river of stars and dark rifts crossing the night. Sailors, caravan leaders, moon-priests, burial clerks, and desert-edge farmers all used it as a road above roads. It is not smooth: it braids, breaks, foams, and darkens like floodwater under two moons. Its bright southern depth is watched for omens; its winter branch runs pale and cold through the high air.
Visible all year in segments. Winter Star-River runs through the cold-season river fields; summer Star-River through northern and southern river gates is brightest.
Visible all year in segments; the Stormblood Tail is highest in southern winter.

Skykeeper reading: Three sovereign lights used by old skykeepers as offices rather than figures: one for dawn, one for north, and one for the high southern summer watch. Nephthysra Glass: spring; Setrimir Diadem: year-round north; Valkhamesh Prime: summer/autumn.

tables.caption_or_previous_text: The Eiršu'neth Comet is a massive, long-period Vishtecu–Hyperu family comet distinguished by its unusually large icy nucleus, high mass, and stable yet dramatic inclined orbit through the outer Belavadös system. With a nucleus about 85 miles (137 km) wide—roughly 10–50 times larger than a typical comet core—and an estimated mass around 500 trillion tons (about 500× that of an average comet), it is one of the most visually and dynamically significant comets in its region. It follows a repeating 6.48 Belavadös-year orbit (≈ 2,139.37 Belavadös days), with a semi-major axis of ~3.48 AU, ranging from a perihelion of 2.08 AU to an aphelion of 4.87 AU. Its 18° inclination above the Celestial Road and carefully positioned crossing points make it a safe, non-impacting body despite its size, periodically producing a spectacular multi-month display as it passes through the inner reaches of its orbit.

sections.heading: Belavadös Night Sky
content: Celestial reference for sky time, moons, wandering worlds, nebula fields, distant stars, sky-lights, and constellations

sections.heading: 5. Two moons in the Belavadös sky
7. Distant stars and sky-lights of Belavadös
Naming and replacement rules used in this document
content: • The bright band crossing the sky is called the Star-River of Belavadös.
• The observing landscape is described as the Great River Valley and its desert-edge skyfields.
• The twelve wandering planets and two moons use the supplied invented names and coordinates.
• The sky analysis keeps historical-style latitude, precession, seasonality, and horizon logic, but is written as Belavadös sky lore rather than a modern archaeological report.

sections.heading: Coordinate system used
content: The sky is described with right ascension and declination. These coordinates function like celestial longitude and latitude. Apparent magnitude uses lower numbers for brighter objects, with negative values being especially bright. Planet and moon distances use AU or kilometers; stellar distances use light-years.

sections.heading: Earth and Belavadös sky time
content: Use Earth dates and Earth time first for players, session schedules, travel timing, event boards, and deadlines. Use Belavadös dates second for lore records, temple calendars, journals, festivals, and immersion. A Belavadös astronomical year is 330.15 Belavadös solar days long, and those solar days are distributed evenly across the Earth year for table play.

For sky calculations, use solar progress rather than the named civil date. The civil calendar still has 330 named dates arranged as eleven 30-date months, while the 0.15 solar-day correction is spread through the year as a tiny clock drift. There is no bonus day or frozen end-period for moons, planets, tides, omens, or the Star-River.

sections.heading: 1. daysInEarthYear = 365, or 366 in a leap year.
3. belSolarDayProgress = earthProgress x 330.15. Use this value for moon phases, planetary positions, tides, constellations, seasons, and sky omens.
4. belCivilDateProgress = earthProgress x 330. Use this value only for the named Belavadös month and date.
5. Belavadös clock time may use the fractional part of belSolarDayProgress x 24.
Player-facing observing log format
content: Write sky events Earth-first, then Belavadös-second: Earth Month Day, Year, local time with UTC label / Belavadös month date, weekday, Belavadös clock, solar-day progress, moon phase, and sky note.

Settlement and province sky notes may include the settlement UTC when the observing site differs from the province primary UTC. Province summaries should show only one or two Earth-style UTC labels, while exact settlement exports can store the UTC chosen by longitude.

sections.heading: Belavadös month cycle for sky records
content: These month names are used for date labels only. A moon, wandering world, tide, season, or sky omen should still be calculated from belSolarDayProgress so the sky remains smooth across the full Earth year.

sections.heading: Historical-style sky setting
content: The analysis assumes a view from approximately 30° N latitude. At 30° N, stars above about +60° declination are circumpolar, while stars below about -60° declination never rise.

The sky looks dark, dense, and sharply structured. With no electric skyglow, the Star-River of Belavadös would have been a major visible feature rather than a faint haze. Bright planets, bright stars, both moons, and future named sky patterns can serve as seasonal markers, navigation guides, calendar anchors, and story-bearing landmarks.

sections.heading: The Star-River of Belavadös
content: The Star-River of Belavadös is the luminous band of unresolved stars and dark rifts crossing the night sky. In summer evenings, it would stretch through the southern gate-and-serpent sectors and climb toward the northern seasonal markers. In winter evenings, it would run near the Bronze Bull region, becoming paler but still visible under dry, dark conditions.

From desert-edge skyfields, the Star-River would not have appeared as a smooth strip. It would have looked mottled, braided, and broken by dark channels. The brightest warm-season section would have been low-to-mid in the southern sky; the higher northern section would have served as a nightly path for visual navigation.

sections.heading: Nebula fields of Belavadös
content: Each nebula uses the same field layout for generator use: coordinate anchor, distance/span, type, dominant colors, layer structure, and texture/components.

sections.heading: Horundar — Sahuagin Deep Gate of Bastveig
3. Celestial inventory
content: This inventory separates fixed stars, upper-atmosphere light, moons, worlds, regions, nebula fields, and the blank constellation placeholder so each part of the sky reference has one clear home.

sections.heading: 4. Constellations
content: These are the sky-names used when the Gods still walked openly across Belavadös, before their prisons, before public ichor engines, before rail bells, portal halls, and industrial skyports taught cities to trust machines more than stars. The names are the names carved into tide stairs, burial ledgers, cairn roads, hearth beams, watchtower lintels, reef shrines, and desert-edge observatories.
Each figure keeps its fixed place in the sky. The names belong to Belavadös. The coordinates preserve the star-path for sky maps, generators, omen records, and night watches.

sections.heading: 4.1. How skykeepers read the fixed heavens
content: Belavadös skykeepers use right ascension and declination as the fixed grid of the upper world. Right ascension runs from 0h to 24h around the sky. Declination rises north or south of the sky-equator. Magnitude records visible brightness; the smaller the number, the stronger the light.

Seasonal movement follows the 330.15 day Belavadös solar year. Civil dates still belong to the eleven named months, but the sky obeys solar progress. Moon phases, tides, wandering worlds, Star-River omens, and constellation seasons move smoothly across the whole year.

The old horizon rule is simple enough for any watchtower: at about 30 degrees north, lights above about +60 degrees stay near the northern sky and lights below about -60 degrees never rise. Other latitudes shift the height of the figures without moving the figures themselves.

sections.heading: 4.3. Seasonal and hemispheric visibility
content: Northern and southern visibility depends on latitude and season. East-west behavior describes how the pattern rises, crosses the meridian, sets, or circles the northern sky during the night.

sections.heading: 4.4. Star layouts and coordinate anchors
content: The following tables preserve the fixed coordinates of each light and sky waypoint. Names are Belavadös names. RA and Dec are the placement anchors used by sky maps, temple charts, observatories, and generators.

sections.heading: 4.5. Skykeeper practice
content: Harbors, caravan wells, funeral roads, terrace farms, reef shrines, and high watchtowers all keep different portions of the same sky. Coastal settlements read Bastveig's Tidehook, Freyseth's Mask, the Star-River, and the two moons for water law. Mountain and inland roads favor Anubaldir's Labyrinth, Enkirael's Warfire, and Setrimir's Diadem. Hearth villages mark Ishtanora's Hearthdrum, while temple singers and roof watchers keep Sokhivar's Lantern.

The old rule remains unchanged: a constellation is a witness. A vow spoken beneath a named figure is never only private. The sky is a ledger, a road, a tide stair, a battlefield, a mirror, a hearth, and a warning. When the Gods were free, this was not metaphor. It was daily survival.

sections.heading: 5. Two moons in the Belavadös sky
content: The lunar system is nested: the larger moon orbits the world, while the smaller moonlet orbits the larger moon and is carried along with it. This creates paired lunar calendars, small bead-like crossings, and a subtle secondary tidal pulse. For Earth sessions, both lunar positions are calculated from belSolarDayProgress, not from the civil month and date.

sections.heading: Lunar phase pacing for Earth sessions
content: Chandratecu-Seleneš phase = (belSolarDayProgress mod 19.20) / 19.20.
Mictlindra-Nannara phase = (belSolarDayProgress mod 2.02) / 2.02.
Use the resulting fraction as the phase position in the lunar cycle. This keeps both moons moving continuously across non-leap and leap Earth years.

sections.heading: 6. Worlds, regions, and comet
content: The worlds orbit their star upon a relatively flat shared plane known as the Celestial Road. Belavadös itself remains the 1.00 AU reference world with a 330.15 Belavadös-day astronomical year; player-facing dates distribute that year evenly across the Earth calendar.

sections.heading: Minor worlds
content: Minor worlds are rounded celestial bodies that share their orbital regions with numerous smaller bodies.

With a nucleus about 85 miles (137 km) wide—roughly 10–50 times larger than a typical comet core—and an estimated mass around 500 trillion tons (about 500× that of an average comet), it is one of the most visually and dynamically significant comets in its region. It follows a repeating 6.48 Belavadös-year orbit (≈ 2,139.37 Belavadös days), with a semi-major axis of ~3.48 AU, ranging from a perihelion of 2.08 AU to an aphelion of 4.87 AU. sections.heading: 7. Distant stars and sky-lights of Belavadös
content: The fixed sky entries are grouped by location and object type. Each table uses the same columns: number, name, type, distance, magnitude, color, RA, Dec, and role/visibility. No formation data is included in this section.
