content: These labels refer to upper-atmosphere light rather than fixed stars. They use no RA/Dec because their appearance depends on magnetic latitude, solar activity, darkness, and weather.

sections.heading: 8. Representative night
content: A representative high-era observing night can be generated by first calculating belSolarDayProgress from the Earth date and local observing time, then placing Chandratecu-Seleneš and Mictlindra-Nannara along their 19.20-day and 2.02-day cycles. A sample scene may place the paired lunar system near RA 06h 15m and Dec +18° to +19°, close to the northern cold-season field and high enough for easy viewing from 30° N.

When the bright inner planet Mardukesh-Huitra is favorably placed, it dominates the evening or dawn sky with pearl-white brilliance. Surixoch-Aresu appears copper-red and lower near twilight. The four ringed planets are not equally easy to interpret with the unaided eye, but under magnification their ring lore becomes central: Vishtecu-Hyperu shows a rose-gold hairline, Enlimitra a frosted silver span, Quetzal-Hermeshu a tilted green-bronze eye, and Varunatl-Kronu a white-ringed blue elongation.

sections.heading: 9. Source and method notes
content: The astronomical logic in this document uses standard sky-coordinate concepts: right ascension, declination, apparent magnitude, latitude-dependent visibility, horizon limits, axial precession, and a 330.15 day Belavadös astronomical year distributed evenly across the Earth year for play. The values are intended for generators, lore notes, sky omens, transit boards, and table-facing observing logs.

No Earth star names are included. The document is intended as a lore-compatible sky reference for Belavadös and as a practical coordinate table for generators; the fixed stars are deliberately placed at remote background distances and several are faint enough to be only partially visible without unusually dark skies or magnification.

sections.heading: Reference ledger
content: • Belavadös sky-time framework: 330.15 day astronomical year, 330-date civil calendar, eleven named months, and Earth-first table play conversion.
• Belavadös celestial register: moons, wandering worlds, comet, celestial regions, nebula fields, distant stars, sky-light labels, and constellation coordinates.
• Sky-coordinate method: right ascension, declination, apparent magnitude, latitude-dependent visibility, horizon limits, and seasonal star movement.
• Lore basis: Age of Open Gods skykeeping, imprisoned-god pantheon memory, pre-industrial temple astronomy, tide law, road law, burial ledgers, and post-ichor infrastructure context.

paragraphs: A complete guide for players and Dungeon Masters
By William Saville, also known as The Transgender T-Rex #TheTransgenderTRex

I built this system to make alignment feel alive instead of frozen. Belavadös treats morality as a profile instead of a label, so characters can grow, slide, fail, recover, and surprise the table in a way that still stays easy to read.

This guide is written for Dungeon Masters, veteran D&D; players who know the old alignment grid, and new players who need a clean way in. I keep the language direct, the rules visible, and the moving parts organized so the system can be learned without losing its depth.
Nothing here is meant to trap a character in a box. Your choices shape your path, and your path reshapes your destiny.
How I want you to use this guide

For DMs, the recommendation is to start with the core axes, then move into the phase rules, and finally the XP sections. These pages establish how to run the system consistently and fairly at the table. For veteran players, the conversion material translates the old two-axis model into the newer four-axis profile system, preserving familiar ideas while adding precision and reducing ambiguity around labels. For new players, the first half of the guide is sufficient to begin play—focus on the axes, review the examples, and understand the difference between fit awards and shift awards. The appendices function as reference material you can consult when needed during play.
What I built this system to do

The system is designed to measure selfishness, lawfulness, cooperation, and honor as separate and independent questions rather than collapsing them into a single alignment label. This allows a character to be lawful yet selfish, cooperative yet dishonorable, or honorable while actively rejecting institutions. The result is a clearer moral shape that is easier to understand and roleplay.

It also emphasizes long-term behavioral patterns over isolated actions. A single act of kindness does not elevate a character into sainthood, just as a single cruel decision does not erase a lifetime of decency. Instead, Belavadös tracks patterns, turning points, sacrifices, betrayals, and repeated behavior to build a more stable and meaningful moral profile.
Quick Roadmap
Audience Guidance
What I built and why it is different

Belavadös treats morality as a living profile rather than a single alignment label. Instead of compressing ethical identity into a fixed nine-box system like traditional D&D alignment, it evaluates a character through four independent axes. Each axis measures a different moral or behavioral pressure, allowing for more nuance and less forced categorization.
Belavadös Moral Axes

This separation is important because real characters rarely fit cleanly into a single moral box. A selfish mercenary is not the same as a dishonorable traitor. A lawful bureaucrat is not automatically cooperative. A cooperative rebel is not necessarily altruistic, and an honorable outlaw may still reject institutional authority entirely. By keeping these axes distinct, Belavadös preserves moral complexity instead of flattening it into broad labels.

The system is also designed to reflect change over time. Each axis can shift as a character grows, deteriorates, or reacts to events. This turns morality into a dynamic record rather than a static label—allowing the system to track a character’s moral biography as they develop, rather than assigning them a single permanent identity.
The four alignment axes
Every character in Belavadös is measured across four independent moral dimensions. Each axis runs from 0 to 3000 points, and 1500 is the neutral center.
If you only remember one thing from this page, remember this: the axes are separate. A character can be high on one axis and low on another without contradiction. That is the heart of the system.
Alignment phases, position steps, and crossing boundaries

I divide every axis into three phases. The low phase, the neutral phase, and the high phase each contain four tracked | positions on the character sheet. That gives me a simple, readable way to show not only where a character stands, | but how far they have moved.
Here are your contents organized into clear tables:
Phase Ranges
Phase Tracking Positions
Point Change System

When a character reaches the edge of a phase, they step into the next phase at the correct corresponding position. A | change of 250 points moves the character one position. Larger changes can leap several positions at once when a | major event deserves it.
Character creation and starting scores

At character creation, or through birth, adoption, awakening, or transformation in game, I let players start in more than | one way. They may take a short scenario based alignment test, choose their alignment manually, or build from a | background, oath, faction, or backstory that clearly points in a direction.

The default starting point for every axis is 1500. That means a new character begins at the neutral center unless the | fiction says otherwise. A DM may shift starting scores by about 100 to 300 points for an ordinary background, and by | larger amounts when divine influence, faction indoctrination, or a very strong concept justifies it.
Strong concept or divine influence Larger shifts are allowed when the fiction justifies it.

I use those modifiers to create distinct personalities without permanently locking anyone into a rigid moral box. The goal is to give the character a believable starting shape, then let play do the rest.
Alignment is dynamic
Your actions continuously shape your moral trajectory. I do not treat alignment as something a player gets stuck with forever. I treat it as something that evolves through play.
A character can begin in one place and end up somewhere very different after one meaningful betrayal, sacrifice, or turning point. That is not a bug in the system. That is the point of it.

In play, I usually think in patterns. One kind act matters, but a repeated pattern of sacrifice matters more. One cruel | choice matters, but a repeated habit of exploitation matters more. The score should reflect the true story of the | character, not a single scene taken in isolation.
Why alignment matters at the table
Belavadös is not just a label system. It is a living reputation system. When the table uses it well, the world can answer the characters in different ways depending on how they have actually behaved.

That means the system can influence trust, fear, admiration, hostility, political standing, access to sacred spaces, rare dialogue, faction invitations, and the kind of legacy people speak about after the session ends.
I want the world to react to the character in distinct ways, not just say they are good or evil. That is why I separate honor from lawfulness and cooperation from altruism.
Running Belavadös in D&D; 5e

Belavadös replaces the rigid old grid with four continuous behavioral axes. That makes it easier to model gradual | change, mixed motives, and morally complicated characters while still staying fully compatible with D&D; 5e roleplay, | factions, magic items, subclasses, divine systems, and reputation mechanics.
When you need to translate old alignment language, I treat it as a threshold question rather than a binary label. Here’s your content organized into a clear table format:
Moral & Behavioral Trait Definitions
Design Interpretation (Belavadös System)
This is still D&D; at the table. I am not replacing the game. I am giving the table a finer tool for reading character identity and narrative consequence.
Rewarding alignment play

I use the same reward logic for both advancement modes. The difference is not what gets rewarded. The difference is | when the points are handed out. My rule of thumb is simple. If a choice is merely on brand, it gets a fit award. If it | genuinely changes the character's direction, it gets a shift award.

A small repeatable behavior should not create a massive shift by itself. A meaningful scene choice should matter. A major moral decision should matter a lot. A campaign defining sacrifice, betrayal, or oath should matter even more.
I also keep the table honest by tying rewards to visible narrative consequences, not to table noise or repetitive point | farming.
Adventuring XP mode
Adventuring XP is the granular version. I use it when the table likes seeing immediate progress and wants alignment to feel like part of the normal rhythm of play.

I award points at the end of each notable scene. I only award for choices with risk, cost, or public consequence. I do | not award for filler talk, repeated probing, or harmless chatter. The system should reward meaningful roleplay, not | table noise.

When a choice fits the current profile, I count that as a fit award. When the choice changes the profile in a way that matters later, I count that as a shift award. A single scene can earn both, but only when both parts are true.
Milestone XP mode
Milestone XP is the chapter based version. I use it when the campaign is narrative heavy, the table is open ended, or the group wants less bookkeeping during a session.

Milestone mode solves the bookkeeping problem without changing the reward logic. I still reward the same kinds of alignment moments, but I log them during play and hand them out at the end of the session, chapter, or story beat.
That keeps the table moving while still making the alignment system feel alive and responsive.
Axis triggers
These triggers are the practical heart of the system. When I look at a scene, I ask which axis the choice touches and whether the action is pushing the character up or down that axis.
5e compatible examples
I keep these examples simple on purpose. They give the DM a clean starting point, but they are not hard limits. The fiction matters more than the exact spell name or combat move.

If an action has both mechanical and narrative weight, I lean into the narrative weight first. Saving an ally in a life or | death moment is not the same thing as casually helping with a small task. The difference should be visible in the | reward.
Translating items, abilities, and world reactions
When old 5e content references alignment, I translate it into thresholds instead of binary labels. That lets me keep the spirit of the item or effect while making the requirement fit the new system.
Traditional requirement | Belavadös translation
A clean DM rule and the veteran player conversion guide

I use alignment as a living reputation system, not a punishment system. I award points only when actions meaningfully | impact story, relationships, faction standing, moral consequences, or character identity. I avoid rewarding repetitive | behavior farming.
For veteran players, the old two axis model still helps as a memory aid. I just split the old idea into four questions so it becomes easier to read mixed characters.

A traditional lawful good hero will usually read as lawful, altruistic, cooperative, and honorable. A chaotic good hero | will usually read as lawless, altruistic, cooperative, and honorable. A character that was simply neutral in the old model | can land in many different places here, because neutral in the old system often meant the label was not trying to | describe that axis very strongly.
New player quick start and DM guardrails
For new players, the easiest way to use this system is to play your character honestly, say why they are acting when the choice matters, and ask me which axis a decision touches if you are unsure.
If two players make the same choice for different reasons, the motive can matter. Keep the table consistent and explain the rule before the campaign starts.

My fairness rule is simple. If the table can explain the award in one sentence, the award is probably clear enough. If it takes five sentences, I log the moment and settle it at the end of the session.
I do not punish imperfect roleplay. I reward intention and consequence. The goal is to help players explore the system, not to turn the table into a test they can fail by accident.
Optional rules and a session tracker
These rules keep the system tight when the campaign needs more control. They are optional, but I use them often when I want cleaner pacing and less argument.
Example Session Tracker
Example starting spreads and archetypes
These starting spreads help me seed characters with a clear moral shape without locking them into a final identity. They are examples, not cages.

I use spreads like these when a player wants a ready made concept that still leaves room to grow. A holy protector, a | criminal mastermind, and a survivalist drifter all begin with very different pressure points, but all of them can still | evolve in play.
Core class tendencies, part 1
These are tendencies, not hard restrictions. I use them as a quick starting point when a player wants a class based profile without choosing every axis by hand.
Core class tendencies, part 2
I keep the same logic for the remaining classes. The point is to give the table a useful baseline, not to limit roleplay or force a character into a box.
Class and subclass mappings, part 1
I use these mappings when a player wants the class identity to lean strongly into one of the four axes. These are narrative tendencies, not restrictions.

Barbarian | Core: Berserker to Chaotic Marauder; Totem Warrior to Neutral Guardian; Zealot to Chaotic Crusader; Wild Magic | to Chaotic Knave; Beast to Neutral Marauder; Ancestral Guardian to Neutral Sentinel; Storm Herald to Chaotic | Defender.

Bard | Core: Lore to Neutral Mediator; Valor to Neutral Champion; Glamour to Chaotic Mediator; Whispers to Neutral | Strategist; Swords to Chaotic Gladiator; Eloquence to Lawful Mediator; Spirits to Neutral Ethicist; Creation to | Chaotic Coordinator.

Cleric | Core: Life to Lawful Guardian; Light to Neutral Crusader; War to Lawful Enforcer; Trickery to Chaotic Strategist; | Death to Neutral Avenger; Grave to Neutral Sentinel; Twilight to Neutral Guardian; Peace to Lawful Mediator; | Forge to Lawful Coordinator; Tempest to Chaotic Defender; Knowledge to Neutral Ethicist; Nature to Neutral | Arbiter; Arcana to Neutral Strategist.

Druid | Core: Land to Neutral Arbiter; Moon to Neutral Warrior; Dreams to Neutral Guardian; Spores to Neutral Ethicist; | Wildfire to Chaotic Defender; Stars to Neutral Sentinel; Shepherd to Neutral Coordinator.

Fighter | Core: Champion to Neutral Warrior; Battle Master to Lawful Strategist; Eldritch Knight to Lawful Sentinel; Arcane | Archer to Neutral Defender; Cavalier to Lawful Guardian; Samurai to Lawful Gladiator; Rune Knight to Neutral | Sentinel; Psi Warrior to Neutral Defender; Echo Knight to Neutral Adapter.
Class and subclass mappings, part 2

The same principle keeps applying. If the story pushes a subclass in a different direction, I let the character drift through roleplay, corruption, redemption, trauma, faction influence, or personal growth.

Monk | Core: Open Hand to Lawful Sentinel; Shadow to Neutral Vigilante; Mercy to Neutral Guardian; Four Elements to | Neutral Arbiter; Kensei to Lawful Gladiator; Astral Self to Chaotic Ethicist; Drunken Master to Chaotic Drifter; Long | Death to Neutral Avenger.

Paladin | Core: Devotion to Lawful Crusader; Ancients to Neutral Guardian; Vengeance to Lawful Avenger; Redemption to | Lawful Mediator; Oathbreaker to Chaotic Marauder; Glory to Neutral Champion; Conquest to Lawful Enforcer; | Crown to Lawful Guardian; Watchers to Lawful Sentinel.

Ranger | Core: Hunter to Neutral Vigilante; Beast Master to Neutral Guardian; Gloom Stalker to Neutral Avenger; Fey | Wanderer to Chaotic Mediator; Horizon Walker to Neutral Sentinel; Swarmkeeper to Neutral Coordinator; | Drakewarden to Neutral Defender; Monster Slayer to Lawful Vigilante.

Rogue | Core: Thief to Neutral Knave; Assassin to Chaotic Avenger; Arcane Trickster to Chaotic Strategist; Swashbuckler | to Chaotic Gladiator; Mastermind to Lawful Strategist; Phantom to Neutral Drifter; Soulknife to Neutral Adapter; | Inquisitive to Lawful Arbiter; Scout to Neutral Drifter.

Sorcerer | Core: Wild Magic to Chaotic Knave; Draconic to Neutral Champion; Divine Soul to Neutral Crusader; Shadow to | Neutral Avenger; Clockwork to Lawful Arbiter; Aberrant Mind to Chaotic Strategist; Storm to Chaotic Defender.
Class and subclass mappings, part 3
These last mappings complete the class reference. I keep the labels and the guidance together so I can read them | quickly at the table.

Warlock | Core: Fiend to Chaotic Renegade; Archfey to Chaotic Drifter; Great Old One to Neutral Strategist; Celestial to | Neutral Guardian; Hexblade to Neutral Avenger; Undead to Neutral Marauder; Genie to Chaotic Champion; | Fathomless to Neutral Sentinel.

Wizard | Core: Abjuration to Lawful Defender; Divination to Neutral Ethicist; Evocation to Neutral Enforcer; Illusion to | Chaotic Strategist; Necromancy to Neutral Avenger; Enchantment to Chaotic Mediator; Chronurgy to Lawful | Arbiter; Graviturgy to Neutral Adapter; Bladesinging to Neutral Gladiator; Scribes to Neutral Collaborator; War | Magic to Lawful Enforcer.
Artificer | Core: Alchemist to Neutral Coordinator; Armorer to Lawful Defender; Artillerist to Neutral Enforcer; Battle Smith to | Lawful Guardian.
Blood Hunter | Core: Ghostslayer to Neutral Crusader; Lycan to Chaotic Marauder; Mutant to Neutral Strategist; Profane Soul to | Chaotic Renegade.
Full alignment profiles, part 1
This appendix is my compact reference for the full profile list. I keep each entry short enough to scan quickly while still showing the name, the axis shape, and the meaning.

Final philosophy
Belavadös is not about assigning permanent labels. It is about consequences, reputation, ideology, personal evolution, social perception, and moral complexity.
Characters are remembered not for what box they were placed in, but for the choices they made when it mattered most. That is the idea I wanted this system to preserve.

If you are a DM, I want this guide to be easy to run. If you are a veteran player, I want it to feel familiar but sharper. If you are new to the table, I want it to feel readable instead of intimidating. That is why I built the system the way I did.
Quick reference
I wrote this guide to be useful at the table. Keep it close, use the pieces you need, and let the characters earn the shape of who they become.

sections.heading: A complete guide for players and Dungeon Masters
By William Saville, also known as The Transgender T-Rex #TheTransgenderTRex
content: I built this system to make alignment feel alive instead of frozen. Belavadös treats morality as a profile instead of a label, so characters can grow, slide, fail, recover, and surprise the table in a way that still stays easy to read.

This guide is written for Dungeon Masters, veteran D&D; players who know the old alignment grid, and new players who need a clean way in. I keep the language direct, the rules visible, and the moving parts organized so the system can be learned without losing its depth.
Nothing here is meant to trap a character in a box. Your choices shape your path, and your path reshapes your destiny.

sections.heading: How I want you to use this guide
content: For DMs, the recommendation is to start with the core axes, then move into the phase rules, and finally the XP sections. These pages establish how to run the system consistently and fairly at the table. For veteran players, the conversion material translates the old two-axis model into the newer four-axis profile system, preserving familiar ideas while adding precision and reducing ambiguity around labels. For new players, the first half of the guide is sufficient to begin play—focus on the axes, review the examples, and understand the difference between fit awards and shift awards. The appendices function as reference material you can consult when needed during play.

sections.heading: What I built this system to do
content: The system is designed to measure selfishness, lawfulness, cooperation, and honor as separate and independent questions rather than collapsing them into a single alignment label. This allows a character to be lawful yet selfish, cooperative yet dishonorable, or honorable while actively rejecting institutions. The result is a clearer moral shape that is easier to understand and roleplay.

It also emphasizes long-term behavioral patterns over isolated actions. A single act of kindness does not elevate a character into sainthood, just as a single cruel decision does not erase a lifetime of decency. Instead, Belavadös tracks patterns, turning points, sacrifices, betrayals, and repeated behavior to build a more stable and meaningful moral profile.

sections.heading: What I built and why it is different
content: Belavadös treats morality as a living profile rather than a single alignment label. Instead of compressing ethical identity into a fixed nine-box system like traditional D&D alignment, it evaluates a character through four independent axes. Each axis measures a different moral or behavioral pressure, allowing for more nuance and less forced categorization.

sections.heading: Belavadös Moral Axes
content: This separation is important because real characters rarely fit cleanly into a single moral box. A selfish mercenary is not the same as a dishonorable traitor. A lawful bureaucrat is not automatically cooperative. A cooperative rebel is not necessarily altruistic, and an honorable outlaw may still reject institutional authority entirely. By keeping these axes distinct, Belavadös preserves moral complexity instead of flattening it into broad labels.

The system is also designed to reflect change over time. Each axis can shift as a character grows, deteriorates, or reacts to events. This turns morality into a dynamic record rather than a static label—allowing the system to track a character’s moral biography as they develop, rather than assigning them a single permanent identity.

sections.heading: The four alignment axes
content: Every character in Belavadös is measured across four independent moral dimensions. Each axis runs from 0 to 3000 points, and 1500 is the neutral center.
If you only remember one thing from this page, remember this: the axes are separate. A character can be high on one axis and low on another without contradiction. That is the heart of the system.

sections.heading: Alignment phases, position steps, and crossing boundaries
content: I divide every axis into three phases. The low phase, the neutral phase, and the high phase each contain four tracked | positions on the character sheet. That gives me a simple, readable way to show not only where a character stands, | but how far they have moved.
Here are your contents organized into clear tables:

sections.heading: Point Change System
content: When a character reaches the edge of a phase, they step into the next phase at the correct corresponding position. A | change of 250 points moves the character one position. Larger changes can leap several positions at once when a | major event deserves it.

sections.heading: Character creation and starting scores
content: At character creation, or through birth, adoption, awakening, or transformation in game, I let players start in more than | one way. They may take a short scenario based alignment test, choose their alignment manually, or build from a | background, oath, faction, or backstory that clearly points in a direction.

The default starting point for every axis is 1500. That means a new character begins at the neutral center unless the | fiction says otherwise. A DM may shift starting scores by about 100 to 300 points for an ordinary background, and by | larger amounts when divine influence, faction indoctrination, or a very strong concept justifies it.
Strong concept or divine influence Larger shifts are allowed when the fiction justifies it.

I use those modifiers to create distinct personalities without permanently locking anyone into a rigid moral box. The goal is to give the character a believable starting shape, then let play do the rest.

sections.heading: Alignment is dynamic
content: Your actions continuously shape your moral trajectory. I do not treat alignment as something a player gets stuck with forever. I treat it as something that evolves through play.
A character can begin in one place and end up somewhere very different after one meaningful betrayal, sacrifice, or turning point. That is not a bug in the system. That is the point of it.

In play, I usually think in patterns. One kind act matters, but a repeated pattern of sacrifice matters more. One cruel | choice matters, but a repeated habit of exploitation matters more. The score should reflect the true story of the | character, not a single scene taken in isolation.

sections.heading: Why alignment matters at the table
content: Belavadös is not just a label system. It is a living reputation system. When the table uses it well, the world can answer the characters in different ways depending on how they have actually behaved.

That means the system can influence trust, fear, admiration, hostility, political standing, access to sacred spaces, rare dialogue, faction invitations, and the kind of legacy people speak about after the session ends.
I want the world to react to the character in distinct ways, not just say they are good or evil. That is why I separate honor from lawfulness and cooperation from altruism.

sections.heading: Running Belavadös in D&D; 5e
content: Belavadös replaces the rigid old grid with four continuous behavioral axes. That makes it easier to model gradual | change, mixed motives, and morally complicated characters while still staying fully compatible with D&D; 5e roleplay, | factions, magic items, subclasses, divine systems, and reputation mechanics.
When you need to translate old alignment language, I treat it as a threshold question rather than a binary label. Here’s your content organized into a clear table format:

sections.heading: Design Interpretation (Belavadös System)
content: This is still D&D; at the table. I am not replacing the game. I am giving the table a finer tool for reading character identity and narrative consequence.

sections.heading: Rewarding alignment play
content: I use the same reward logic for both advancement modes. The difference is not what gets rewarded. The difference is | when the points are handed out. My rule of thumb is simple. If a choice is merely on brand, it gets a fit award. If it | genuinely changes the character's direction, it gets a shift award.

A small repeatable behavior should not create a massive shift by itself. A meaningful scene choice should matter. A major moral decision should matter a lot. A campaign defining sacrifice, betrayal, or oath should matter even more.
I also keep the table honest by tying rewards to visible narrative consequences, not to table noise or repetitive point | farming.

sections.heading: Adventuring XP mode
content: Adventuring XP is the granular version. I use it when the table likes seeing immediate progress and wants alignment to feel like part of the normal rhythm of play.

I award points at the end of each notable scene. I only award for choices with risk, cost, or public consequence. I do | not award for filler talk, repeated probing, or harmless chatter. The system should reward meaningful roleplay, not | table noise.

When a choice fits the current profile, I count that as a fit award. When the choice changes the profile in a way that matters later, I count that as a shift award. A single scene can earn both, but only when both parts are true.

sections.heading: Milestone XP mode
content: Milestone XP is the chapter based version. I use it when the campaign is narrative heavy, the table is open ended, or the group wants less bookkeeping during a session.

Milestone mode solves the bookkeeping problem without changing the reward logic. I still reward the same kinds of alignment moments, but I log them during play and hand them out at the end of the session, chapter, or story beat.
That keeps the table moving while still making the alignment system feel alive and responsive.

sections.heading: Axis triggers
content: These triggers are the practical heart of the system. When I look at a scene, I ask which axis the choice touches and whether the action is pushing the character up or down that axis.

sections.heading: 5e compatible examples
content: I keep these examples simple on purpose. They give the DM a clean starting point, but they are not hard limits. The fiction matters more than the exact spell name or combat move.

If an action has both mechanical and narrative weight, I lean into the narrative weight first. Saving an ally in a life or | death moment is not the same thing as casually helping with a small task. The difference should be visible in the | reward.

sections.heading: Translating items, abilities, and world reactions
content: When old 5e content references alignment, I translate it into thresholds instead of binary labels. That lets me keep the spirit of the item or effect while making the requirement fit the new system.

sections.heading: A clean DM rule and the veteran player conversion guide
content: I use alignment as a living reputation system, not a punishment system. I award points only when actions meaningfully | impact story, relationships, faction standing, moral consequences, or character identity. I avoid rewarding repetitive | behavior farming.
For veteran players, the old two axis model still helps as a memory aid. I just split the old idea into four questions so it becomes easier to read mixed characters.

A traditional lawful good hero will usually read as lawful, altruistic, cooperative, and honorable. A chaotic good hero | will usually read as lawless, altruistic, cooperative, and honorable. A character that was simply neutral in the old model | can land in many different places here, because neutral in the old system often meant the label was not trying to | describe that axis very strongly.

sections.heading: New player quick start and DM guardrails
content: For new players, the easiest way to use this system is to play your character honestly, say why they are acting when the choice matters, and ask me which axis a decision touches if you are unsure.
If two players make the same choice for different reasons, the motive can matter. Keep the table consistent and explain the rule before the campaign starts.

My fairness rule is simple. If the table can explain the award in one sentence, the award is probably clear enough. If it takes five sentences, I log the moment and settle it at the end of the session.
I do not punish imperfect roleplay. I reward intention and consequence. The goal is to help players explore the system, not to turn the table into a test they can fail by accident.

sections.heading: Optional rules and a session tracker
content: These rules keep the system tight when the campaign needs more control. They are optional, but I use them often when I want cleaner pacing and less argument.

sections.heading: Example starting spreads and archetypes
content: These starting spreads help me seed characters with a clear moral shape without locking them into a final identity. They are examples, not cages.

I use spreads like these when a player wants a ready made concept that still leaves room to grow. A holy protector, a | criminal mastermind, and a survivalist drifter all begin with very different pressure points, but all of them can still | evolve in play.

sections.heading: Final philosophy
content: Belavadös is not about assigning permanent labels. It is about consequences, reputation, ideology, personal evolution, social perception, and moral complexity.
Characters are remembered not for what box they were placed in, but for the choices they made when it mattered most. That is the idea I wanted this system to preserve.

If you are a DM, I want this guide to be easy to run. If you are a veteran player, I want it to feel familiar but sharper. If you are new to the table, I want it to feel readable instead of intimidating. That is why I built the system the way I did.

paragraphs: BELAVADÖS
Ichor Math Compendium
A canon-ready mathematical framework for divine electrochemical fluid, fluid-electric discharge, skyship power, Thundercoil charge, healing, mutation, and industrial scaling.

Core design law: Ichor is treated as a divine bioelectrochemical suspension: part redox-flow electrolyte, part hypergolic propellant analogue, part ionic liquid, part plasma precursor, and part sacred contaminant. Every equation below is a worldbuilding model, not a real-world chemical procedure.
Working Contents
1. Canon framing and safe use of the math
2. Measurement system, units, symbols, and source keys
3. Ichor states, grades, and engine roles
4. Master variables and dimensional checks
5. Energy release, potency, and efficiency
6. Separated-reagent reaction kinetics
7. Redox-flow and fuel-cell behavior
8. Conductivity, resistance, coils, and charge packs
9. Plasma sheath, arcs, and fluid-electric jets
10. Nozzle, pressure, and pressure-washer behavior
11. Rocket, thrust, specific impulse, and skyship impulse math
12. Thermal management, cooling, and runaway containment
13. Pressure vessels, membranes, rupture, and fatigue
14. Lift, buoyancy, sail-field coupling, and skyship power
15. Thundercoil scaling from hand weapons to ship engines
16. Light, flame color, chemiluminescence, and cyan signature
17. Healing, mutation, dosage, toxicity, and divine resonance
18. Purity, contamination, corruption, and legal grading
19. God-specific ichor coefficients
20. Worked examples and worksheets
21. D&D 5e-style conversion notes
22. Source register and citation key
1. Canon Framing and Safe Use of the Math

This compendium gives Belavadös a repeatable mathematical language for ichor. It keeps the horror intact while making the technology feel engineered: priests harvest, refiners denature, guilds certify, captains budget, mechanics maintain, smugglers contaminate, and engines obey numbers even when the numbers are haunted.

The central canon rule is separation. Ichor becomes safest when divided, diluted, bonded, cooled, grounded, and metered. It becomes dangerous when opposing fractions touch directly, when membranes tear, when catalysts overheat, when prayer resonance overloads the charge, or when living divine residue begins behaving as if it wants something.

The math below intentionally avoids real-world procedural recipes. Real chemical examples are used only as analogies: combustion explains fuel and oxidizer logic, hypergolic propellant behavior explains contact ignition, flow batteries explain separated liquid charge, fuel cells explain chemical-to-electrical conversion, plasma explains conductive luminous gas, and rocket equations explain momentum exchange. In-world materials use fictional names such as fresh ichor, black ichor powder, breath-salt, storm-brass, aether niter, saintglass membrane, godsblood brine, void char, and hunger ash.
Canonical sentence: Ichor is not lightning in a bottle; it is divine hunger forced into an electrochemical bookkeeping system.
2. Measurement System, Units, Symbols, and Source Keys

Belavadös engineers use mundane units when building hulls, tanks, nozzles, wheels, and masts. Temple engineers add divine units for potency, resonance, purity, hunger, and corruption. A mixed system works best for play: real equations handle scale, while Belavadös coefficients bend the results toward fantasy without losing internal consistency.
3. Ichor States, Grades, and Engine Roles

Ichor is strongest when the setting distinguishes state from grade. State says what form the substance is in. Grade says how safely civilization can use it. A drop of fresh godblood, a spoon of black powder, and a tank of denatured catalyst oil may all come from the same source, but their equations belong to different machines.
4. Master Variables and Dimensional Checks

All ichor math should pass a simple check: units must make sense. If an equation creates energy, the result should be joules or an in-world energy unit. If it creates thrust, the result should be newtons or a force-like rating. If it creates risk, the result should be dimensionless. This lets you bend equations without breaking the world.
E_available = m_i * e_i * Pi * eta_reaction * eta_containment
Available energy equals ichor mass times usable energy density, reduced by purity, reaction efficiency, and containment losses. Use this for fuel budgeting and city-scale power.
P_output = E_available / t
Power is energy delivered per time. A tiny cell can hold large energy but still be low power if it releases slowly.
Risk = Severity * Probability * Exposure * Moral_Load
A worldbuilding risk equation. Moral_Load lets divine exploitation make legal fuel politically safer but ethically heavier.
Safety_Margin = Rated_Limit / Operating_Load
Keep this above 1.5 for civilian machines, above 2.0 for passenger skyships, and above 3.0 for temple-prison infrastructure.
5. Energy Release, Potency, and Efficiency

Ichor energy density should not be constant. Common industrial catalyst should be weaker than fresh divine blood because it has been denatured for safety. Starved-god ichor should be powerful but unstable. Primordial ichor should produce absurd energy and apocalyptic instability. This gives engineers a reason to prefer legal fuel even when smugglers can offer stronger black-market fuel.
A tabletop potency index. Pi is purity, H is hunger instability, Psi is resonance load, and G_s is a god-source multiplier.
E_burst = E_available * min(1, IPI/8) * eta_burst
Burst energy is the portion of stored energy that can be released quickly. High energy does not always mean high burst unless the engine can vent it.
6. Separated-Reagent Reaction Kinetics

Belavadös engines work because separated components are stable alone and dangerous together. Instead of writing recipes, use reaction-rate math. The reaction rate rises with concentration, temperature, catalyst surface, and resonance. Safety comes from limiting contact area, limiting time, and preventing backflow.
rate = k_eff * [I]^a * [B]^b * A_contact
The reaction rate increases with ichor fraction concentration [I], breath-salt/brine concentration [B], and contact area. Use only fictional reagents.
k_eff = k_0 * exp(-E_a / (R*T_eff)) * (1 + C_cat + Psi - S_stab)
The effective rate constant rises with heat, catalyst, and resonance, and falls with stabilizers. This is the safe worldbuilding version of temperature-sensitive reaction math.
T_eff = T + T_arc + T_prayer + T_friction
The engine can overheat chemically, electrically, ritually, or mechanically.
7. Redox-Flow and Fuel-Cell Behavior

The strongest mundane analogue for safe ichor power is the redox-flow battery: charged fluids remain in separate reservoirs and produce power as they pass through an electrochemical reactor. Belavadös adds divine resonance, living catalyst, and rune membranes. If the fluids exchange charge through a membrane, the engine works. If they mix directly, the result is fluid lightning.
V_cell = V_0 + K_god + K_rune - (R*T / (n*F)) * ln(Q_reaction)
A Belavadös Nernst-style cell voltage. V_0 is mundane electrochemical potential, K_god is divine source bonus, K_rune is inscription quality, and Q_reaction is the concentration ratio term.
P_cell = V_cell * I_cell * eta_electrical
Electrical power from an ichor cell. Use for lamps, locks, weapons, medical tools, and ship control circuits.
E_tank = V_tank * C_charge * V_cell * eta_storage
Flow-cell energy scales with tank volume and charge concentration. This makes large ships possible without giving every handheld item ship-scale output.
Crossover_Loss = k_membrane * Area_membrane * DeltaC * t
Membrane leakage over time. Old or damaged membranes slowly poison the opposite reservoir.
8. Conductivity, Resistance, Coils, and Charge Packs

Thundercoil technology becomes consistent when a charge pack is treated like a compact ichor flow cell feeding a coil. Current creates the control effect; overcurrent creates heat, arc flash, nerve stun, pack ejection, or catastrophic coil breach.
R_path = L_path / (sigma_i * A_path)
Resistance falls when conductivity or conductor area rises. Long, thin, corroded paths overheat.
P_heat = I_cell^2 * R_path
Heat buildup in coils and conduits. This is why overloading a Thundercoil should call for corruption risk.
E_pack = N_charges * E_shot / eta_pack
Pack energy equals number of charges times energy per shot, adjusted for pack efficiency.
Recovery_Time = Heat_Load / Cooling_Rate
Use this for recharge rests, cooldown periods, and large-ship firing cycles.
9. Plasma Sheath, Arcs, and Fluid-Electric Jets

Fluid electricity is a two-phase effect: charged droplets carry mass and momentum while the surrounding air becomes ionized enough to glow and conduct. The droplet stream behaves like a pressure jet; the plasma sheath behaves like lightning; the rune nozzle forces both to stay coherent long enough to cut, weld, thrust, or stabilize.
E_field = V_d / gap
Electric field strength rises as voltage rises or arc gap narrows. High field strength ionizes air more easily.
Jet_Cohesion = (rho_i * v_j^2 * d_nozzle) / (surface_tension + turbulence + wind_shear)
A worldbuilding ratio: high inertia and good nozzle design keep the jet coherent; turbulence and crosswind break it apart.
Arc_Risk = max(0, E_field / E_breakdown - Grounding_Margin)
Arc risk rises when electrical stress exceeds the local breakdown threshold and grounding is poor.
Plasma_Glow = Ionization_Fraction * m_dot * v_j * Color_Coefficient
The visible glow follows ionization, flow, speed, and the god/metal color signature.
10. Nozzle, Pressure, and Pressure-Washer Behavior

At tool scale, ichor discharge resembles an extreme pressure washer because liquid mass is forced through a small aperture. At ship scale, the same principle becomes a pressure column and thrust plume. The core equations are pressure, area, flow rate, velocity, and momentum.
v_j = sqrt(2 * DeltaP / rho_i) * eta_nozzle
Ideal pressure-jet velocity from pressure difference and fluid density, reduced by nozzle losses.
m_dot = rho_i * A_nozzle * v_j
Mass flow through a nozzle. Tiny nozzles can still be violent when pressure is huge.
F_recoil = m_dot * v_j + (p_exit - p_air) * A_exit
Thrust/recoil from a liquid-plasma nozzle. This is the same skeleton as rocket thrust with a denser working fluid.
Cutting_Index = DeltaP * A_focus * Arc_Factor / Stand_Off_Distance
Tool-scale cutting power. Close focus cuts metal; wider focus pushes or stuns.
11. Rocket, Thrust, Specific Impulse, and Skyship Impulse Math

Rocket math is useful for Belavadös engines when the ship throws mass backward, downward, or sideways. It should not be the only skyship lift model because metal galleons also use keel lattices, aetheric pressure, and ichor-thread sails. Use rocket equations for burst, climb, acceleration, recoil, and fuel budgeting; use hybrid lift equations for steady cruise.
F_thrust = m_dot * v_e + (p_e - p_a) * A_e
General rocket-like thrust: mass flow, exhaust velocity, and pressure correction.
I_sp = v_e / g_0
Specific impulse in seconds. In-world, this becomes an efficiency rating for discharge lenses and reaction throats.
Delta_v = v_e * ln(m_0 / m_f)
Use only for propellant-limited maneuvers, emergency burns, and long climbs where the ship loses significant reaction mass.
F_vertical_total = L_aero + L_aether + T_vertical + B_buoy - W
A skyship climbs when this total is positive and descends when it is negative.
a_vertical = F_vertical_total / m_ship
Acceleration follows Newton second law after all lift and weight terms are counted.
12. Thermal Management, Cooling, and Runaway Containment

Heat is the simplest way to make the technology feel real. Every reaction and every current path produces heat. Every safe machine must remove heat faster than it accumulates. If heat accumulates, viscosity drops, reaction rate rises, membrane leakage rises, and corruption risk climbs.
Q_heat = E_released * (1 - eta_useful)
Waste heat is whatever released energy does not become useful thrust, light, electricity, lift, or work.
DeltaT = Q_heat / (m_coolant * c_p)
Temperature rise from heat added to coolant.
Cooling_Rate = h * A_radiator * (T_engine - T_air)
Convective cooling approximation. More radiator area and more temperature difference remove heat faster.
Runaway_Index = (Heat_Generation / Heat_Removal) * (1 + H + contamination)
Above 1.0, heat is building faster than it is removed. Above 1.5, passenger systems should shut down.
13. Pressure Vessels, Membranes, Rupture, and Fatigue

Ichor machines need pressure math because fluid electricity is not purely mystical. Tanks, tubes, membranes, and reaction throats are physical objects. A pressure-safe engine room should look full of ribs, hoops, rivets, sacrificial seams, glass inspection windows, and redundant shutters.
sigma_hoop = P_internal * r_tank / t_wall
Thin-wall pressure vessel hoop stress. Larger radius and pressure increase stress; thicker walls reduce it.
Safety_Factor_pressure = sigma_allowable / sigma_hoop
Pressure safety factor. Passenger engines should have generous margins.
Fatigue_Damage = Sum(n_i / N_i) * (1 + corrosion + H)
Cycle damage from repeated pressure and thermal pulses. Divine hunger acts like a fatigue multiplier.
Membrane_Load = DeltaP + Charge_Gradient + Prayer_Shear
Saintglass membranes fail mechanically, electrically, and ritually.
14. Lift, Buoyancy, Sail-Field Coupling, and Skyship Power

A metal galleon skyship should not hover on decorative exhaust alone. Belavadös lift is a hybrid of thrust, aetheric lattice force, aerodynamic lift, sail-field coupling, and sometimes limited buoyancy. This keeps the visuals naval and steampunk while letting the physics stay legible.
W = m_ship * g_B
Weight equals mass times local gravity. Belavadös can use Earthlike g unless a region changes it magically.
L_aero = 0.5 * rho_air * V^2 * S_sail * C_L
Lift from moving air over sails or wing-like surfaces. Works best in cruise, not at a dead hover.
B_buoy = rho_air * g_B * V_displaced * phi_liftgas
Buoyancy from displaced air or enclosed lift gas. In Belavadös, phi_liftgas may include aether-vapor enhancement.
L_aether = lambda_a * P_lattice / v_leak
Worldbuilding lift: the keel lattice converts power into upward pressure. Higher lambda_a means better runes and better ichor-thread coupling.
P_hover_min = W^(3/2) / sqrt(2 * rho_air * A_effective)
Rotor/actuator-disk inspired hover power. For skyships, A_effective is the combined belly-bell, lattice, and sail-field area.
15. Thundercoil Scaling from Hand Weapons to Ship Engines

Thundercoils and skyship engines should feel like one technology family. A pistol is a tiny metered coil. A rifle has longer acceleration rails. A shock-bomb is a deliberately unstable pack. A ship engine is a cathedral-sized Thundercoil with redundant reservoirs, pumps, nozzles, discharge lenses, cooling loops, and grounding halos.
P_total = Sum(P_cell_i) * eta_sync
Multiple cells combine only as well as their synchronization and grounding allow.
Breach_Radius = k_breach * (E_burst)^(1/3)
Blast radius scales sublinearly with burst energy. This keeps large engines terrifying without making every failure world-ending.
16. Light, Flame Color, Chemiluminescence, and Cyan Signature

Belavadös cyan is not ordinary blue paint. It is the visual signature of ionized ichor salts, storm-brass catalysis, and divine charge release. Other gods and grades can shift flame color without changing the basic engine family.
Photon_Energy = h * c / wavelength
Shorter wavelengths carry higher photon energy. Use this as the logic behind different flame colors.
Glow_Output = Chem_Energy * Phi_light * eta_visibility
Cold-light output depends on chemical energy, quantum-like light yield, and optical clarity.
17. Healing, Mutation, Dosage, Toxicity, and Divine Resonance

Healing and mutation should use dose math rather than simple morality. Small controlled doses can trigger repair. Medium impure doses intoxicate, distort, or addict. High doses overwhelm identity. Repeated exposure accumulates spiritual load even when the body survives.
Dose = mass_absorbed / body_mass
Basic dose scaling. Larger creatures need more substance for the same concentration, but divine resonance can override size.
Healing_Effect = Dose * Pi * G_heal * eta_body - Toxicity
Healing rises with dose and purity but falls when toxicity outruns repair.
Mutation_Risk = Dose^n * H * (1 - Stabilization) * Exposure_Count
Mutation risk climbs nonlinearly with dose, hunger instability, poor stabilization, and repeated exposure.
Addiction_Load = Sum(Dose_i * Euphoria_Factor * Memory_Imprint)
Track this for political horror: miracles can create dependency even when they work.
18. Purity, Contamination, Corruption, and Legal Grading

Purity is not the same as safety. Legal skyship fuel is usually less pure than fresh ichor because it has been diluted and bound. Black-market fuel often advertises purity while hiding unstable hunger ash, cult residue, stolen hospital ichor, or counterfeit brine.
Effective_Purity = Pi_true - contamination - hunger_ash - water - counterfeit_salt
Inspection guilds care about effective purity, not seller claims.
Corruption_Chance = Base + 0.25*H + 0.2*Psi + 0.2*contamination + 0.15*overload - maintenance
A tabletop probability score. Convert to a d20 or d100 threshold as desired.
Legal_Risk = Scarcity * Purity * Source_Crime * Political_Attention
A smuggler equation for how badly authorities will respond.
19. God-Specific Ichor Coefficients

God-source coefficients let ichor feel tied to the pantheon without creating twenty-two separate rulebooks. Each god modifies one or two parameters: energy density, conductivity, healing, mutation, stability, color, or resonance. Engineers care because the source changes the math; priests care because the source changes the sin.
20. Worked Examples and Worksheets

These examples use fictional values. They are meant to help you keep scale consistent from scene to scene. Replace numbers freely when the story needs a vessel to be humble, noble, military, cursed, ancient, or experimental.
20.1 Lantern Cell
m_i = 0.05 kg, e_i = 0.5 MJ/kg, eta = 0.20
A tiny safe lantern brine cell.
Enough for low light or a short bright pulse, not a weapon.
20.2 Thundercoil Hand Pack
10 shots * 2,000 J/shot = 20,000 J useful output
A practical pack can stun or control without being artillery.
If eta_pack = 0.4, stored energy = 20,000 / 0.4 = 50,000 J
Heat and losses explain cooldowns and corruption rolls.
20.3 Skyship Emergency Lift Column
Required upward force reserve = 0.15 * W
A 15 percent emergency reserve gives a heavy ship enough climb margin after cargo shifts.
P_required = F_vertical * v_climb / eta_lift
The engine must spend power both to hold weight and to climb.
20.4 Breach Risk Check
Corruption_Chance = 0.05 + 0.25H + 0.20Psi + 0.20contamination + 0.15overload - maintenance
Convert decimal to percentage. If H = 0.4, Psi = 0.2, contamination = 0.1, overload = 1, maintenance = 0.1, risk = 24 percent.
21. D&D 5e-Style Conversion Notes

The equations should not slow down play. Use them behind the screen to decide whether a device is safe, unstable, expensive, or spectacular. In combat, convert the math into charge counts, DCs, damage dice, conditions, cooldowns, and corruption rolls.
Source Register and Citation Key
This compendium uses bracketed source keys in tables and formulas so the worldbuilding text stays readable. The sources are listed here rather than crowded into every paragraph.
Supplemental Mathematical Annexes

These annexes expand the compendium into reusable design tables. They are meant for writing, game design, engineering-flavored lore, and consistent scaling across lanterns, Thundercoils, skyships, prison refineries, portals, hospitals, and city infrastructure.
Annex A. Master Equation Catalog
Annex B. Ichor Device Design Worksheet
Use this worksheet whenever a new ichor item, machine, or engine enters the setting. It keeps invented objects consistent with the core chemistry and physics logic.
Annex C. Refineries, Yield, and Denaturing Math

Refining turns living divine fluid into something industry can meter. The refinery never simply maximizes purity. It seeks stable yield: enough potency to be useful, enough denaturing to be legal, and enough filtration to keep engines from hearing the god too clearly.
Yield_refined = m_raw * Recovery_Rate * (1 - Spoilage - Ritual_Tax - Security_Loss)
How much usable catalyst/brine remains after legal harvesting, transport, filtering, temple claims, and black-market leakage.
Stability_Index = Denaturing + Filtration + Binding_Oil + Storage_Coolness - Freshness - Hunger - Contamination
Positive values mean the batch behaves like industrial material. Negative values mean the batch behaves like a living omen.
Price = Base * IPI * Scarcity * Legal_Risk / Stability_Index
More power, scarcity, and legal danger raise price; stability lowers maintenance cost.
Annex D. Industrial Scale Ladder
Annex E. Thundercoil Numerical Pack

For play, keep Thundercoil math behind the curtain. A charge pack needs only four numbers: useful energy per shot, safe current, heat debt per shot, and breach threshold. All other drama can be generated from those.
E_shot = Damage_Tier * Control_Tier * Focus_Factor * 500 J-equivalent
A fictional conversion that scales damage and control without claiming real weapon energy.
Heat_Debt_per_Shot = E_shot * (1 - eta_coil) + I^2*R*t_pulse
Heat debt explains why repeated shots, wet weather, and overload cause failures.
Safe_Shots_Before_Cooldown = Heat_Capacity / Heat_Debt_per_Shot
Use this to decide charge count or cooldown frequency.
Overload_Multiplier = P_requested / P_safe
At 1.0 the weapon is operating at rating. At 1.5 it should complain. At 2.0 it should become a story problem.
Annex F. Skyship Ichor Use from the Fuel Master Perspective

The fuel master does not think like a pilot. They think in tanks, purity, thermal debt, membrane health, and how much of the god is still listening. Their equations turn a dramatic skyship scene into an operational ledger.
Daily_Fuel_Burn = (P_cruise*t_cruise + P_hover*t_hover + P_hotel*t_day) / (e_i*Pi*eta_reaction)
Daily fuel demand for route planning.
Emergency_Reserve = 0.25*Daily_Fuel_Burn + Storm_Allowance + Cargo_Shift_Allowance
Reserve should include weather, docking delays, and cargo surprises.
Tank_Segregation_Index = Number_of_Independent_Tanks / Critical_Fractions
A ship is safer when one tank breach cannot mix every dangerous component.
Field_Blackout_Time = E_backup / P_essential
How long a ship can keep lift, lights, steering, and medical wards alive after main reactor failure.
Annex G. Medical and Mutation Calibration
Medical ichor is a regulated poison that happens to heal at the right dose. The same equation can save a patient, addict a noble, mutate a soldier, or expose a hospital smuggling ring.
Therapeutic_Window = Effective_Healing_Dose / Toxic_Dose
Wide windows are safe medicine. Narrow windows require expert healers and monitoring.
Identity_Shear = Dose * H * Psi * Dream_Exposure / Will_Anchor
A roleplay metric for whether the patient remains fully themselves after divine healing.
Regeneration_Rate = k_body * Dose * Pi * G_heal - Scar_Tissue - Curse_Load
Use for long-term recovery, scars, missing tissue, or divine strings attached.
Annex H. Portal, Rail, and City Grid Math

Ichor should not power only vehicles. The same math supports rail wards, city lights, hospital beds, locks, messenger systems, portal gates, factories, and divine prisons. The difference is release rate and risk tolerance.
Grid_Load = Sum(P_homes + P_industry + P_wards + P_transit + P_emergency)
A city grid is a sum of loads, not a single magical battery.
Reserve_Fraction = (P_capacity - Grid_Load) / Grid_Load
Cities with low reserve fraction experience brownouts, ward flicker, and political panic.
Line_Loss = I^2 * R_line * distance_factor
Long rail or ward lines lose power through resistance and require substations.
Portal_Stability = P_field * Rune_Alignment / (Mass_Transfer + Distance + Weather + Interference)
A route gate is stable only when the field power and inscriptions outrun load and disruption.

Each god modifies one or two parameters: energy density, conductivity, healing, mutation, stability, color, or resonance. Engineers care because the source changes the math; priests care because the source changes the sin.

The equations should not slow down play. Use them behind the screen to decide whether a device is safe, unstable, expensive, or spectacular. In combat, convert the math into charge counts, DCs, damage dice, conditions, cooldowns, and corruption rolls.
